text: 8 a.m. The CEO announces Pulsar and Meridian are merging, and you are leading the integration. You have a hundred questions; he has zero answers. Accept?
HR brings the lists: 214 people at Pulsar, 187 at Meridian, and 23 job titles match down to the comma. Who do you talk to first?
Meridian's coffee machine has moved into the shared kitchen next to yours. This morning the queue split perfectly along company lines. Join the other queue?
Pulsar's sales director wants Meridian's clients moved to his people "by tomorrow." The clients haven't been told yet. Slow him down?
Meridian's accountant politely notes their fiscal year starts in April, yours in January. The board wants a report by Friday. How do you reconcile?
right: January it is, end of story

text: 9:40 p.m. You've spent three hours comparing two org charts and catch yourself drawing arrows on a napkin. Dinner is waiting. Finish at least this department?
In the unofficial chat someone posts: "Word is everyone from Meridian gets cut by spring." You're in the chat too, and everyone can see you've read it. Reply?
The guard won't let a Meridian employee in: her pass is from "the other system." Behind her, a queue of colleagues with the same passes. What do you say?
Meridian's IT director demos their CRM: "It's better than yours, just admit it." Your team is rehearsing the same speech next door. What now?
At home you're asked how your day went. You start explaining the difference between two vacation-approval systems. A minute in, your partner yawns. Keep going?
The office manager asks which mugs stay in the shared kitchen: Pulsar blue or Meridian orange. The cupboard fits only one set. Decide by lunch.
A Pulsar veteran, twenty years with the company, catches you at the elevator: "I've survived three reorgs and I'll survive you." He's smiling. Probably joking. Your move?
left: Invite him onto the task force

text: Legal reports that merging supplier agreements means re-signing 340 contracts. "Doesn't have to be all at once," he adds, without much hope. Where do you start?
right: All at once, from a template

text: First integration committee meeting. Twenty-two members, a four-page agenda, zero decisions. Time's up. What do you propose?
In the evening your kid asks for help with a school project: "How to merge two classes into one." You catch yourself starting a RACI matrix and a comms plan. Stop?
right: Go all the way to a Gantt chart

text: The brand manager brings four new logo options. Three show two arrows colliding head-on. "It's about synergy," he explains. Your pick?
A Meridian employee asks point-blank: "Should I start job hunting or not?" Her role is on the duplicate list, but nothing's decided. What do you say?
10:15 p.m. Merging two staff spreadsheets, you find three Sergei Ivanovs with the same title. One of them, it seems, left last year. Sort it out now?
right: Flag it and go to bed

text: Morning inbox: 140 emails titled "Re: Re: Fwd: Integration — question." Half of them say "Same question here." How do you dig out?
The CFO wants "synergies in numbers" by Monday. So far the only saving is one shared printer. What goes in the report?
The sysadmin says the email domains will merge overnight into Saturday. Some messages might go missing for a few hours. Warn everyone?
On the way home you play a podcast about mergers. The host says 70% of integrations fail. Switch it off?
A Meridian intern asks which of the two group chats to use for sick-day notices now. You're not sure yourself. What do you say?
Meridian's former CEO, now your deputy for integration, arrives at the stand-up with his own agenda. It's thicker than yours. What do you do?
A courier delivers a thousand business cards with the new logo. On the back, Pulsar's old phone number, which dies tomorrow. Hand them out?
left: Send them back for a reprint
right: Hand out and fix by pen

text: The two accounting teams argue over who runs the combined books. Both have done it "twenty years without a single error." Who gets it?
In the evening you notice you keep saying "here at Pulsar" instead of "here." Third time today. Did Meridian notice?
left: Watch your words from now on

text: The cleaner asks whose plants to water: Pulsar's ficuses or Meridian's cacti. Turns out they have different care schedules.
right: Rota with one from each side

text: A project manager suggests calling the integration "Project Phoenix." Half the office points out phoenixes burn first. Approve?
A neighbour calls in the evening: "You're a merger expert, right? How do we combine two garden plots?" You've done mergers all day. Help?
right: Promise to drop by at the weekend

text: Your calendar shows nine back-to-back meetings: "Sync," "Sync on the sync," and "Pre-sync." No lunch. What goes?
Meridian's warehouse lead says their forklifts keep left, Pulsar's keep right. The warehouses merge on Monday.
A Pulsar employee complains the new colleagues "smile too much in meetings — it's suspicious." What do you do?
left: Set up a coffee with them

text: Mum calls to ask if you got cut in the merger. You explain you're the one running it. "Well then be extra careful," she says.
HR wants to send everyone a 40-question "How are you feeling after the merger?" survey. People already joke it's a survival test.
The analyst reports one client appears in the two CRMs as "Daisy LLC," "LLC Daisy," and "Daisy (do not call)." There are eight thousand such records.
Third evening in a row you're last out. The guard already knows your favourite tea. Is that sweet or worrying?
Turns out both companies booked the same room at the same time: one system calls it "Baikal," the other "Room 3." Who yields?
The CEO asks when we'll have "one culture." You show a six-month plan. "Faster? By the holiday party?" The party is in three weeks.
right: Explain it doesn't work that way

text: Meridian's team lead runs stand-ups standing; your people sit, with biscuits. The joint team has been stuck for ten minutes. How do you settle it?
Evening, editing the all-staff deck. The slide "What won't change" so far lists only "Lunch hours." Enough?
right: Add a couple of upbeat ones

text: Meridian's shuttle driver asks if he'll be driving people to the new office. He's run the old route for fifteen years and knows everyone by name.
The press office wants a comment on the rumour that Meridian's regional office is closing. Half-true: it's moving, not closing.
Your fitness tracker says 2,400 steps today, 2,000 of them between the two companies' floors. Evening walk?
Morning notification: "Your access to Meridian systems has expired." In an hour you're chairing their meeting about access. What now?
Procurement wants to switch the stationery supplier to "ours" right away. Meridian loves its pens, and someone's already posted a poem about them.
Two marketing heads — one from each company — show up together and ask you to decide who's in charge. They look at you expectantly.
right: A month of working together first

text: You dream about merging two fridges, and one holds all your emails from the week. You wake at 4:30. Get up or go back to sleep?
left: Try to go back to sleep

text: An evening chat war: Pulsar people thumbs-up everything, Meridian people read that as passive aggression and use hearts. Step in?
left: Post a joke guide to reactions

text: Going to bed, you remember you never answered Meridian's chief accountant. He wrote at 6:02 p.m. It's 11:10. Reply now?
The marketing door sign says "Pulsar Marketing." Underneath, someone has taped "and Meridian." The tape is crooked. What now?
The support lead says clients are calling both old numbers and reaching agents who can't see their history. The queue is growing.
A Meridian employee asks why Pulsar celebrates birthdays with cake while Meridian gives a day off. "So now we just get cake?"
right: Cake for all, no day off

text: In the evening Pulsar's laptop refuses Meridian's VPN. The second laptop doesn't have your email. You sit between two laptops like a pianist.
HR asks what to call roles now. At Meridian everyone is a "lead specialist," at Pulsar a "manager." The salaries run the other way round.
Meridian's best developer hands in his notice: "Nothing personal, I just hate uncertainty." A competitor made an offer. Try to keep him?
The committee asks each department to describe its processes within a week. Sales sends one word: "We call." Accept it?
left: Sit down and map it with them

text: Evening text from an unknown number: "It's Lena from Meridian logistics, sorry it's late — are we really being cut?" Reply?
Watching a show where two royal houses unite through a wedding, you notice their integration is moving faster than yours. Finish the episode?
Reception reports both companies ordered water for Monday from different suppliers. Forty bottles are lined up at the entrance.
The agent offers a new office big enough for both companies. One catch: it's across town for all of Meridian. Sign it?
Training wants a session called "How to Love the New CRM." Three hours. Mandatory. Friday afternoon. Approve?
Friday, 7:30 p.m. You've finally finished the warehouse merger plan. It's 64 pages. Who's going to read it on Monday? Cut it to two?
left: Cut it down over the weekend

text: The CEO's assistant needs a seating plan for the joint meeting. "Just don't seat the former directors next to each other." There are five of them and the table is round.
Marketing wants merch: T-shirts saying "We're one team now." There's a budget, but sizes are due tonight. Collect them?
Meridian's lawyer reminds you each transfer needs the employee's consent. Four hundred papers, nervous people. How do you run it?
An old friend invites you fishing on Saturday. You meant to finish the role matrix. "The fish won't wait," he says. Neither will the matrix.
Turns out Meridian works 9 to 6, Pulsar 10 to 7. In the joint department half the people arrive to empty desks.
The controller finds both companies pay for the same cloud subscription. Twice. For the third year. Who cancels it?
left: Cancel it yourself in an hour

text: Meridian's sales head asks you not to touch his team till quarter-end: "We're hitting target, don't break it." The schedule says integration starts now.
Your dog demands a walk the moment you open an email titled "URGENT: new structure." He sits by the door and stares at you.
A Pulsar employee is hurt: her desk went to a Meridian newcomer and she was offered a draughty spot by the window. "Is that a sign?" she asks.
right: Promise to fix it by Monday

text: Security wants to merge the access systems, but everyone needs new photos. The photographer is only available tomorrow, 8 to 9 a.m.
The agency presents three names: "Pulseridian," "MeriPulse," and "The Company." The last one, they say, is "bold." Your pick?
You notice your "keep key people" list has no one from accounting. Without them, nobody gets paid. Review it tonight?
Your cat is asleep on the laptop showing the department merger sheet. The cursor sits in a cell labelled "Cut?" The cat purrs. Wake him?
The new joint pass works only on Pulsar doors. Meridian lets you in on the old one. The guard shrugs sympathetically.
The external auditor asks why one Meridian business trip has twelve expense reports. You learn about it at the same time he does.
Pulsar's quality team keeps processes in hundred-page manuals. Meridian keeps them in Marina's head. Marina is on vacation. What now?
A friend wants to see a comedy. You say your life is already a comedy about two offices. "All the more reason to unwind," she insists.
Morning meeting on seating. Meridian wants open plan, Pulsar wants offices. The designer's compromise: "semi-open offices" with curtains.
The analyst built a "Unity Index" dashboard. It rose 3% because both companies now lunch at the same café. Show it to leadership?
Pulsar names delivery routes by colour, Meridian by number. The shared board now shows "Green 14." Drivers are confused.
At 10 p.m. the CEO sends a seven-minute voice note: "I've got an integration idea." The idea: merge everything into one department. Listen to the end?
Today you had lunch away from the laptop for the first time this week — with two arguing marketing heads. Does that count as rest?
The anonymous "Merger Uncensored" channel posts a draft of your org chart. The wrong one, two weeks old. What do you do?
The HR director proposes a buddy scheme: every Meridian newcomer gets a Pulsar buddy. So far, two volunteers.
left: Sign up as a buddy yourself

text: IT asks which email format to use: first.last or f.last. The companies did it differently, and three people now collide.
Home late, you tell your flatmate about "synergy." He asks if it's like soup from two pots. You pause to think.
right: Jot the idea for a deck

text: Survey results are in. Staff's top worry isn't layoffs — it's that "Meridian's Friday pizza will get cancelled." Your call.
The migration lead wants the weekend: "We'll move CRM data on Saturday if you're reachable." Saturday is your niece's birthday.
left: Stay on call from the party

text: Staff get two weekly newsletters — one from each company. One says all is well; the other says it's complicated.
At dinner a notification arrives: "Meeting 'Final decision on coffee machines' moved to 7:00 a.m." Is this really that important?
You realise that in a month of integration you've never asked your own team how they're doing. They're nervous too, just quietly. Message them now?
Travel rules differ: Meridian takes the train, Pulsar flies. Tomorrow you're visiting their branch. How do you go?
Finance shows department mergers save money if six roles go. The six are the best salespeople from both companies. The numbers look lovely.
6:45 a.m. The alarm goes off and you remember: today you announce which of two department heads stays. You're the one announcing. Get up now?
left: Up and out for a run

text: Morning news: last night's migration moved all Meridian clients into the shared CRM — minus their phone numbers. Sales starts at 9.
right: Let them use the old system

text: On the train you meet a Meridian employee who now travels to the new office. He grumbles that his commute is an hour longer. Sympathise?
The morning newsletter went out with Pulsar's logo at the top and Meridian's sign-off at the bottom. Someone's already calling it "the sandwich." Fix it?
The joint dev stand-up runs 40 minutes: everyone explains not just what they did, but how "we used to do it." Cut it short?
At breakfast you see in the chat that Meridian staff have all worn matching orange T-shirts today "as a sign of unity." Their own colour. Say something?
Reception asks how to answer the phone: "Pulsar, hello," "Meridian, hello," or "Good morning, how can I help?" The new name isn't approved yet.
Pulsar's chief engineer catches you at the door: "If I end up under their engineer, I'm out." Their engineer apparently said the same.
In the shared lot, Pulsar parks diagonally and Meridian parallel. By 9:15 nobody has a space. Your proposal?
A Pulsar intern asks: the internship was promised by Pulsar, and Pulsar is about to disappear. Will he still get a job?
Two salespeople from different companies are fighting over a client both call "theirs." The client calls you to ask who he should talk to now.
left: Pick one, give the other a bonus

text: The wellbeing coach offers group sessions called "Anxiety of Change." Twelve signed up, all from Pulsar. Widen it?
The COO wants to merge warehouses early, "while everyone's motivated." By your reading, motivation is running on fumes.
Meridian's back office still prints every invoice and signs it in blue ink. Pulsar does it all electronically. Invoices now arrive both ways.
Meridian's regional director complains he learned about the merger from the news. He's genuinely hurt. You've got a 15-minute window.
Procurement says the merged company has 14 office-cleaning contracts. Four are for the same office. How many stay?
On your evening run, thinking about the "target operating model," you realise at kilometre three you're heading to Meridian's old office. Keep going?
The family chat is planning a holiday. You propose "integrating" both options — beach and mountains. Silence. A minute later your sister writes: "Are you at work?"
Your new pay scale is tidy and fair. But it cuts the bonus for three people. You've been putting off that email for three evenings.
left: Send it and call each one

text: Your partner offers to help with the logo: "I was good at drawing in school." The sketch on the back of a receipt isn't even bad. Take it?
left: Show the agency for a laugh

text: At 9 p.m. the lawyer emails: "Found a five-year exclusivity clause with a supplier in Meridian's contract." It breaks the procurement plan.
Evening, looking at the calendar: the vacation you booked before the merger is in two weeks. Integration is in full swing. Go?
The analyst shows sales fell 4% after the office move. He suspects the new coffee machine, which brews slower.
The culture council proposes new values. There are eleven, and two contradict each other: "Speed" and "Thoroughness." Approve?
A key Meridian client calls: "New manager, new contract, new invoice. Be honest — does anyone remember me?"
left: Invite him to meet in person

text: Pulsar's team lead wants code reviews in the merged team done "our way — in pairs." Meridian had one person reviewing everything. Decide now.
right: Try their way for a month

text: In the morning a Meridian employee is standing at your desk holding a box: "They told me this is my spot now." Nobody told you.
right: Sort it with the office manager

text: On the morning call, half have Pulsar backgrounds, half Meridian. The CEO wants "one background" by tomorrow. Who makes it?
Pulsar's accountant arrives in tears: in the new system her reports are now labelled "Import_old_2." Twenty years of work — "old."
On your way in you spot a competitor's billboard: "While they merge, we work." Clever. Annoying. Tell the team?
Meridian's storekeeper shows the notebook where he's tracked stock by hand for 15 years. "I won't be retyping this into your system." It's a thick notebook.
You bring croissants for the merged team. Nobody from Meridian takes one: they don't eat at their desks. Awkward.
At the strategy session both sides draw the company's future. Pulsar draws a rocket, Meridian a ship. The facilitator suggests "a flying ship."
You're running training on the new CRM. "Any questions?" Every hand goes up. First question: "Can we have the old one back?"
In the evening you read the company's reviews on a jobs site. A new one: "The merger is rough, but at least someone explains things properly." That seems to be about you.
The sysadmin writes at 11:30 p.m.: "Network merge done. Almost. The 3rd-floor printer only prints for Meridian." Critical?
In the evening you draw up the list of people leaving after the merger. Nine names. You want to say goodbye to each personally. That takes a week.
You dream the two logos on the town-hall screen start fighting. You wake at 3 a.m. Write it down for a presentation?
left: Note it and go back to sleep

text: The CEO wants a video by Wednesday: "We are one family." The staff in it should hug. Many object.
Pulsar's finance folks use pivot tables, Meridian's write two-screen formulas. The joint report won't open for anyone. What now?
left: Run a training on one standard

text: Your sister calls to complain about her boss. Listening, you recognise yourself last week in her boss. Admit it?
You stay late to help both teams move furniture in the new office. Your legs ache, but the desks are in place. Photo for the newsletter?
Meridian's marketing approves posts within an hour; Pulsar takes a week with three sign-offs. The merger post has been stuck for four days.
An assessment consultant wants to test all managers from both companies. 120 questions, including "What kind of tree are you?"
Meridian sends you their acronym glossary: 212 entries. For them "MCP" means "monthly client plan"; for you it's "Monday coffee pause."
The photographer for the all-company photo arrives at 8:30. Thirty of four hundred people showed up. The rest are "stuck in traffic." Shoot?
Your Meridian deputy came in early and has already handed out tasks to the team. Good tasks. But you didn't approve them.
left: Thank him and agree on rules

text: Pulsar's coffee machine broke on moving day. Pulsar staff are convinced it's sabotage. Meridian's machine says nothing and keeps brewing.
An employee transferring from Meridian brings an 18-signature clearance form. Half the signatories have already left.
The "hello@" inbox got 600 emails overnight. It used to be read by one Meridian person who left last Friday. Who reads it now?
Meridian's CFO agrees to step back as an adviser if he can keep his office. You need it for a meeting room. Haggle?
In the project chat two people are arguing over "integration" versus "consolidation." It's been going since 11; now it's 2 p.m. Everyone else is silent.
Meridian orders A4 paper, Pulsar orders Letter. The printers are shared now and the margins come out top or bottom at random.
An account manager wants to email all clients: "Nothing will change." Actually everything will change except the politeness.
You organise mixed lunches: each table half Pulsar, half Meridian. Ten minutes later people have re-sorted themselves the old way.
right: Let them sit where they like

text: HR asks whether the transfer order can say "due to the merger" instead of "due to reorganisation." Softer, but legal objects.
Your nephew asks what you do. "Integration lead," you say. "Like someone who joins Lego from different sets?" Pretty much.
An evening ad: "How to Survive a Merger," a 40-hour online course with a certificate. You're living through it in real time.
In the evening you remember you never decided whose gym discount stays. Both companies are waiting. Trivial or not?
Today you said "Good question, I'll get back to you" three times. The notebook now holds twenty such questions. Tackle them now?
Dinner out with your partner. At the next table people are loudly discussing "a merger where everything's a mess." They're your staff.
You set your messenger to Do Not Disturb. Five minutes later the CEO writes: "I see you're busy. But it's really urgent."
The board wants "integration progress" as a percentage. You have no idea how to measure culture in percent. What do you give them?
IT asks which messenger stays: the one where Pulsar jokes in GIFs, or the one where Meridian discusses budgets. The vote came out 50/50.
A Pulsar employee asks to move to a Meridian team: "It's calmer there and they go home earlier." His manager will be furious.
right: Talk him out of it for now

text: Pulsar had board games on Fridays, Meridian had karaoke. The shared office has one room. Both sides wait for your decision.
You're stuck in traffic and late for your own meeting on "Punctuality in the Merged Company." Start without you?
On his first day in the shared office, a Meridian newcomer sits alone eating a sandwich in a meeting room. You walk past with your coffee. Stop?
Meridian's veterans won't learn the new system: "We retire in two years." The system must be live by spring.
The marketing director wants to spend the budget rebranding fences at every warehouse. Meanwhile staff are short of new laptops.
You notice you've stopped answering friends: 46 unread in their chat. The latest: "Are you alive?" Reply?
Washing up in the evening, you brainstorm names for the merged company: "Sink," "Sponge," "Drying Rack." Write one down?
At the evening Q&A an anonymous question comes in: "Why does management get its own coffee machine while we queue for two?" Giggles in the room.
Riding home on a scooter, you're overtaken by a courier with a Meridian ad on his bag. The ad is out of date. Call marketing?
An employee gets an automatic email: "You've been transferred to Department 0000." Department 0000 doesn't exist. He messages you in a panic.
You're invited to a meeting on how to reduce meetings. Duration: an hour and a half. Go?
Meridian's remote employees hear every bit of news last because Pulsar discusses it at the water cooler. They're asking for "fairness."
left: Post every decision in a channel
right: Invite them in for a week

text: IT wants to shut down Meridian's old system for good this weekend. Meridian's accounting hasn't exported its archive yet.
Team leads from both companies ask to split their joint team back into two. "More efficient." You suspect it's just calmer.
Evening bike ride. You vow not to think about work. Five minutes later you've worked out how to merge the two warehouses. Stop and note it?
Today, for the first time, you settled a dispute between two directors in five minutes, and both left happy. You want to tell everyone. Brag?
Grandma calls to complain her clinic merged two offices too and now the queue is longer. She wants advice from the "expert."
Internal comms wants the company values in verse. First line: "Pulsar, Meridian, one plan, one team." It gets worse.
An access audit shows 40 former Meridian staff can still log into the shared drive. One of them logged in yesterday.
Morning walk-round of the new office. In one corner Meridian has strung fairy lights; in another Pulsar has a poster: "Silence = productivity." Leave it all?
Your Pulsar assistant and your deputy's Meridian assistant are both managing your calendar. At 10:00 you have two meetings in two buildings.
Morning elevator with six Meridian employees. Everyone goes quiet when you step in. It's a long way to the twelfth floor. Say something?
Forty parcels arrive addressed to "Meridian, 4th floor." There's no Meridian 4th floor anymore — it's Pulsar accounting now.
The risk director arrives at 8 with a question: who signs payments over a million in the merged company? There's been no answer for a month.
You try Meridian's coffee for the first time. It's much better than yours. Admitting it publicly would open Pandora's box.
Turns out Thursday appears twice in the shared meeting schedule: once in Meridian's regional time zone. Half the team missed the stand-up.
Meridian's security guard says he used to greet every employee by name. In the new building he knows no one. He's sad.
You must announce who heads the merged sales team. The pick is from Meridian. Pulsar isn't expecting it. How do you break it?
The Meridian floor in the new office has old-type sockets. Pulsar laptops won't plug in. Someone has brought an extension cord from home.
At breakfast your partner asks why you're smiling at your phone. You're reading about two accountants from rival companies who bonded over crosswords.
IT reports they can't find one of Meridian's servers after the move. It seems to hold five years of sales history.
A Meridian marketer shows their brand has three times the recognition. You've already ordered signs with the new name. Halt the order?
The treasurer explains the companies use different banks, and transfers between them take three days. Payday is tomorrow.
The process working group has mapped 18 processes in a month. Each in two versions. The third, "target" version hasn't been started.
A Pulsar warehouse worker asks why Meridian colleagues got warm gloves and they didn't. Same warehouse, same winter.
Legal reports the new name's trademark is already held by a bakery in another city. The signs are printed.
You realise you haven't had a glass of water all day — but five coffees from two different machines. Is that integration too?
A Meridian employee writes in the evening: "Thanks for standing up for our pizza today. Small thing, but it meant something." Unexpectedly, you feel warm.
The team orders pizza to finish the process map tonight. They invite you to stay. You're expected home in an hour.
Reading a business book at bedtime, you fall asleep on the chapter "Culture eats strategy for breakfast." Will it eat you by morning?
Your dad calls to say he lived through a merger in the 90s: "Back then one coffee maker decided everything." He offers advice. Listen?
At 11:40 p.m. Meridian's logistics head posts a warehouse photo to the shared chat: "We did it!" Only his own people reply. Chime in?
You promised yourself evening English lessons. The textbook has sat under a stack of "Target Model v7" printouts for three weeks. Dig it out?
Your upstairs neighbours are renovating and arguing about where the wardrobe goes. "Just like work," you think. Knock?
Today you told an employee "Your role is safe," and in the evening learned it's being merged after all. He'll arrive happy tomorrow. Call now?
Finance finds Meridian has paid monthly rent for a water cooler that doesn't exist. It was removed three years ago. The payments continue.
You're asked to build a joint talent pool. Pulsar has 30 candidates, Meridian has 3 — it seems Meridian just didn't hear about it.
Quality wants to audit every Meridian process before merging. That's three months. The process merger is in one.
In the canteen Pulsar takes soup and Meridian takes salads. The cook asks why soup runs out but salads don't. Should he be part of the integration?
right: Tell him to make more soup

text: On a call with the regional office, Meridian staff are in ties, Pulsar in hoodies. The CEO jokes about dress code. Someone is offended.
The IT director suggests ditching both CRMs and buying a third, "neutral" one. Both teams look at you with horror and hope.
You're ten minutes late and the stand-up has started without you — your Meridian deputy is running it. Running it well. Slip in quietly?
In the smoking area you overhear: "The new structure's already approved, they just didn't tell us." It isn't approved. What do you do?
In an hour, the all-company town hall. The CEO wants to open and "dispel all fears." His speech begins with the word "optimisation."
A Meridian client emails you "by mistake": "I hear things are collapsing there. Should I renew?" Answer it yourself?
You hand out new business cards. A Pulsar employee refuses: "I carry my old one — it has my first office on it." Insist?
right: Ask him to use the new one

text: In the managers' chat a Pulsar manager accidentally posts: "So, which of them are we keeping?" The chat has 40 people, half from Meridian.
The company counsellor says he's getting more messages than usual. All about the same thing: "I don't know what's coming." He asks for clear timelines.
At a team meeting someone asks: "Aren't you afraid you'll be let go once the integration's done?" Everyone freezes.
In the evening the kids fight over the games console. Out of habit, you propose "a console committee with a rotating chair." They stare at you.
Colleagues in the regional office ask for a 9 p.m. call — it's already morning there. You've been on your feet all day. Agree?
You catch yourself getting irritated with a Pulsar veteran who resists everything new. Then again, you don't like the new email client either. Admit it?
10 p.m. email: "URGENT: who has the keys to Meridian's warehouse?" Apparently the man who left on Friday.
right: Deal with it in the morning

text: You pause your show to check email. Half an hour later the show is still paused and you're writing about two accounting standards.
Rereading this morning's all-staff email, you spot a typo in the word "integration": "intergation." Four hundred people read it.
left: Fix it in the next email

text: At the gym you run into Meridian's sales director on the next treadmill. He clearly wants to talk about his team. You just wanted to run.
An evening call from a headhunter: "I see you're running a tough merger. Fancy a calm company?" It's a good offer.
You host dinner for both leadership teams. An hour in, everyone has drifted to their own end of the table to talk football. Football unites. Is that enough?
You open your home laptop to order groceries, and it offers to "merge two accounts." Click Yes?
For the first time today you couldn't remember which company the person you just spoke to came from. Is that a good sign?
The night migration crew orders pizza. Two different pizzas arrive: each company ordered its own. Both with pineapple.
You open the stand-up with "How's everyone doing?" Only Pulsar people answer. Meridian isn't used to such questions at work.
Meridian's assistant brings you 32 powers of attorney to sign. "The old ones expired, and suppliers have to be paid today."
7:30 a.m. You wake with a clear thought: "Why two procurement teams when we could have one strong one?" Good thought — and someone will be very upset.
right: Sit on it for a week

text: A Pulsar call-centre agent says Meridian's clients are politer and talk longer. The call targets are slipping. Advice?
Pulsar's chief accountant suggests "quietly absorbing" Meridian's accounting. Quietly won't work: they sit on the other side of the wall.
A morning business paper writes about the merger and misquotes you: "We'll cut everything extra." You said "extra processes."
Cleaning in the new office starts at 8 with vacuums. Pulsar arrives at 10 and never notices. Meridian arrives at 8 and suffers.
right: Ask them to bear it a month

text: The bank calls: "A payment for Pulsar landed in Meridian's account, and one for Meridian in Pulsar's." Same amount. Coincidence?
left: Sort it out with the bank
right: Net them off and move on

text: Meridian's HR asks to keep their mentoring programme: "It's the one thing we're proud of." Expensive, but it works.
Pulsar's designers use one app, Meridian's another. Neither can open the other's files. The website mock-ups are due.
A Pulsar branch manager won't let integration consultants on site: "I have targets, they have surveys." The consultants are offended.
You're invited to an agenda-less meeting titled "Important." Inside: eight people who want to discuss why the new office has no microwave.
A Meridian safe turns up, and nobody remembers where the key is. Finance is sure the contracts are inside. Security offers to crack it.
A marketing employee proposes a podcast, "The Merger from the Inside," with honest stories. Legal doesn't know yet.
Pulsar's warehouse refuses Meridian's shipments: "Their pallets are different." By two centimetres.
Evening call from the Meridian veteran you talked into staying: "You know, I've been thinking… I like the new system." First call like that.
For the third time tonight you open the redundancy list and change nothing. Nothing needs changing — you're just anxious. Close it?
Over dinner, a lawyer friend hears about your trademark clash with the bakery and starts explaining how she'd handle it. Dinner goes cold.
Watching a cartoon with the family where two towns fight over a bridge, your kid asks: "Is your work like that?" Answer honestly?
Before bed you write tomorrow's to-do list: 34 items, twelve of them "talk to someone about someone." Trim it?
At a morning "get to know you" session everyone gives their name and former company. The last woman says: "I'm from 'ours.'" Applause.
The internal name poll closed this morning. "Pulsar" won — because Pulsar has more staff. Meridian is silent.
Meridian writes memos on letterhead; Pulsar writes them in one word in chat. This morning you got a letterhead memo consisting of "OK."
The landlord of Meridian's old office offers a discounted renewal. The new office isn't ready. Meridian's staff hope to stay put.
The CEO wants a lobby wall of the "best employees of the merged company." The list is all Pulsar. He hasn't noticed.
The analyst asks how to define an "active client." Pulsar: bought within a year. Meridian: opened an email within a month. The report is off by half.
The sales head wants special terms for his stars so they won't defect. He has eight stars; Meridian has two.
Today you said "no" to the CEO and kept your job. Reason to celebrate or to lose sleep?
In the evening you're sent the song Meridian sang at every party. They want it to become everyone's. It's about "our small but proud Meridian."
At the supermarket you find yourself comparing two identical yoghurt brands, deciding which would survive a merger. The shopper behind you coughs.
On your morning run you meet Meridian's CFO. He suggests running together on Tuesdays "and checking numbers on the way." Agree?
A Pulsar IT tech refuses to handle Meridian's tickets: "Not our system." There are already 27 tickets this morning.
A life-size Meridian exhibition stand sits at the entrance. Someone wants to bin it, but apparently it's "part of the family." Your call?
left: Put it in a company museum

text: You're training managers on "How to talk about change." One asks: "What if I don't understand what's changing myself?"
Finance has credited 12 million in savings from "shared meeting rooms" in the synergy report. The number is clearly made up.
right: Keep it, the board will love it

text: Security wants all Meridian staff re-vetted. No such check for Pulsar. People will notice.
Over morning coffee the CEO asks if we can manage "without any cuts." Yesterday he asked for "savings of a third." Clarify?
In the new office Pulsar cards open Meridian's doors, but not the reverse. Meridian staff knock and wait. Not nice.
An industry site reports: "Pulsar–Meridian merger stalling." Source: an anonymous employee. Half the office has read it.
A box of chocolates from Meridian's accounting is on your desk with a note: "Thank you for not rushing us." You were about to rush them.
Installers arrive at 7 a.m. to take down Meridian's sign. Meridian staff come outside to photograph it, some in tears.
The CEO got two sales reports this morning, one from each company. Figures for shared clients differ by 30%. He calls you.
The new building's elevators can't cope: all of Meridian arrives at 9, all of Pulsar at 10. Proposal: shift one group to 9:30.
Pulsar's and Meridian's lawyers read the same contract clause differently. Each is certain. You need a decision by 3 p.m.
A new hire who joined after the merger asks: "Which company am I from?" She genuinely wants to know where to go for lunch.
right: Invite her to lunch with you

text: The strategy director wants to brand the first post-merger year "The Year of Unity." On T-shirts, mugs, and email signatures.
HR finds Meridian gets 31 days' leave, Pulsar 28. Pulsar staff have already heard and ask about the extra three.
Meridian's staff council requests a meeting: "We want to hear about layoffs first." You don't know everything yourself.
left: Meet and share what you know

text: An expensive external consultant delivers his report. Main recommendation: "Merge the companies." That's what you're already doing.
Meridian's product team ships every Friday; Pulsar's ships quarterly. The joint product broke the very first Friday.
Audit discovers Pulsar has bought paper from Meridian through a middleman for three years. You're one company now; the middleman is still there.
A high-performing Meridian employee asks for a promotion: "At Pulsar, these numbers get you promoted." She's right.
right: Include her in the general review

text: The committee wants a report on "staff mood" by Thursday. You suggest just walking the floors and talking to people.
The seating meeting runs till 8 p.m. One question remains: who sits next to the printer. Everyone's exhausted.
You promised your kid you'd build a model ship tonight. But there are 30 pages of IT integration agreement to read. The ship has waited since morning.
You think: if the merger cut you, you'd finally get some sleep. A scary and cosy thought. What do you do with it?
The CEO calls at 8:30 p.m.: "I hear Meridian is unhappy. Is that true?" You know it is, and you know why.
At evening yoga the instructor asks you to "unite the two halves of your body into one whole." You hear an integration plan. Relax?
You've been added "by mistake" to Meridian's unofficial chat. They're discussing that you're "decent enough, but from Pulsar." Leave?
Planning a home renovation, you catch yourself wanting a responsibility matrix for the builders. They didn't sign up for that.
In the evening you scroll through photos from the first month of integration. You're holding a laptop in every one. Two in one of them. Food for thought?
Meridian's key engineer says he's been offered a job in another city. He'll decide by tonight. Meet him this morning?
You're handed two onboarding guides: Pulsar's is 80 pages, Meridian's is a postcard saying "Welcome." New hires start tomorrow.
Meridian's e-signatures don't work with the new system. Twenty contracts must go out by noon.
Your new Meridian deskmate turns on the radio at 9: "We always did this, it perks people up." You're not perking.
right: Put up with it a week

text: The designer sends the final logo. It looks suspiciously like Pulsar's, rotated 90 degrees. Meridian will notice.
Meridian's buyer shows her supplier is 15% cheaper, but Pulsar has used its own for ten years. That supplier is the director's friend.
At the budget meeting it emerges Meridian plans in thousands and Pulsar in millions. The summary sheet says you're bankrupt.
An internal warehouse-manager role opens. Two apply, one from each company. Both are good. You're asked to decide.
The removals company demands extra: "You didn't mention Meridian has a piano." Meridian really does have a piano in the lobby.
For the first time in a month you left on time. On the metro you feel guilty, though everything's done. What now?
An entrepreneur friend says over dinner: "A merger's like moving in with a new flatmate. Sort the fridge out first." You laugh. It's true.
left: Tell him about the coffee machines

text: Friday, 6:30 p.m. The team invites you out to mark the end of the week — both companies together for the first time. You planned a quiet night.
A departing Pulsar employee sends a farewell email to everyone: "Thanks to all — except the integration." It's forwarded to you.
1 a.m. You lie awake wondering if you picked the right head for the merged department. It's already been announced. What now?
left: Get up and write down doubts
right: Give it a chance and sleep

text: Morning war over the AC: Pulsar likes 20°C, Meridian likes 25°C. Someone hid the remote. You're asked to become "Keeper of the Remote."
The new office's meeting rooms need names. Pulsar wants planets, Meridian wants cities. The signs print today.
Meridian puts a quote of the day in email signatures; Pulsar uses just name and number. Leave room for quotes in the new one?
Labels appear on the shared fridge shelves this morning: "Pulsar" and "Meridian." Someone stuck "Nobody's" on the top shelf. There's a cake on it.
You accidentally sent a "Managers only" email to "All staff, both companies." Subject: office space reduction schedule.
Monday. On your desk: a resignation from the Pulsar department head you considered a pillar of the integration. He writes: "I'm tired." Call him?
A Meridian employee asks if their "parents leave at 4 p.m. on Fridays" rule will survive. Pulsar has nothing like it.
right: Promise it in the new policy

text: The new system demands a password change: 16 characters, a symbol, a number, and the name of your first company. Which do you type?
Someone from Pulsar posted a meme about the "takeover" in the announcements channel. It's funny; Meridian doesn't think so. Forty reactions in ten minutes.
Logistics discovers both companies use the same haulier on different rates. Meridian's is 20% cheaper.
Your Meridian deputy proposes meetings standing up: "They'll be shorter." The CEO can't stand long — his back.
Both companies have football teams. Sunday's tournament allows only one entry. Both want to play.
right: Let them play each other first

text: Pulsar's intranet asks for a Meridian intranet password to show merger news. The news is that the intranets have been merged.
Meridian's finance team converts at the start-of-month rate, Pulsar's at the deal-date rate. It surfaces 40 minutes into the meeting.
Meridian allowed dogs at work. A corgi has arrived at the new office; half of Pulsar is taking photos. The other half is sneezing.
The bank wants consolidated financials for last year. The merged company didn't exist last year. The bank insists.
Meridian's support writes formally with a signature; Pulsar's uses emojis. Clients complain about a "split personality."
Pulsar's top seller says he'll quit if his clients go to "the Meridian newbies." The newbies sell better.
Facilities wants the new office in grey and beige "so nobody's offended." Dull, but neutral.
A senior Meridian developer asks why a Pulsar junior now reviews his code. "He's good, but I'm 50 and I wrote this module."
right: Explain it's one rule for all

text: Pulsar lunches at 1, Meridian at 12. A 12:30 meeting leaves everyone hungry. Someone's already eating in the meeting.
In the evening you realise you spent the whole day on mugs, labels and the AC remote. The strategy didn't move. Is that failure?
At the first joint party the host announces a quiz: "Who knows the other company best?" The prize is a day off. Join in?
Your kid is writing a report on "Jobs of the Future" and asks if "company integrator" will still exist in ten years. You're not sure it exists now.
right: Joke and send them to bed

text: Your Meridian deputy writes: "Can I run the sales meeting alone tomorrow? I want to show we can do it too." Trust him?
Walking home, you catch yourself counting the steps to Meridian's old office. Nobody asked you to. Stop?
You suddenly realise you like Meridian. Their calm, their coffee, their crossword-loving accountant. Pulsar would be embarrassed to admit it. Say it aloud?
A courier brings a box to your home: "Meridian's know-how, 10 years." Sent by the departing director "with best wishes." Three kilos of paper.
The former Meridian director who left after the merger calls: "How are my people?" He really cares. You're tired but touched.
Twenty minutes to the first joint town hall. Meridian's chief wants to speak first; so does Pulsar's. One microphone.
The shuttle brings Meridian staff in 40 minutes late on the new route. The meeting is under way; they need answers.
Meridian's marketing director agrees to stay but wants the title "brand co-founder." No such title exists.
Testing the merged order system: Meridian's test order goes through; Pulsar's ships to Mongolia. Literally: delivery address Ulaanbaatar.
right: Launch and fix on the fly

text: Meridian's regional office works in another language. Two translators handle integration documents, and "optimisation" comes out differently in each.
Evening maths: 63 meetings this month, 41 decisions, 90 cups of coffee. Decisions per meeting are falling. Time to change something?
Today you made a decision neither Pulsar nor Meridian liked. Maybe that means it's fair. Or not.
Falling asleep, you keep hearing the CEO: "Integration is a marathon." You've been sprinting for two months. Change something?
Fourteen Meridian vacation requests land on your desk this morning — all for the same week. Moving week. Coincidence?
The ground-floor barista already knows: Pulsar orders americano, Meridian cappuccino. He asks what you'll have "so nobody's offended."
A sticky note on your monitor this morning: "Thanks for listening. Anonymous from Meridian." Next to it: "And from Pulsar too." Nice.
right: Tidy up and get to work

text: Morning stand-up: Meridian's office in another city sees you from the waist up, the camera points at the ceiling, and they hear every other word.
The mystery shopper's report: a customer was sent from Pulsar's office to Meridian's and back again. He left without buying.
The deputy CEO for finance wants to freeze hiring "just in case." Two teams have been waiting a month for new people.
Pulsar staff learn their health insurance is switching to Meridian's plan. Many haven't booked their existing appointments.
left: Extend the old plan a month

text: A Pulsar client asks if invoices will now come from Meridian. "I fell out with them once." What do you say?
The agency pitches an ad: "two trees grown together at the roots." Expensive video. Your CEO wants a rocket.
The warehouse lead reports the merged depot is running, but stocktaking turned up 400 extra chairs. Nobody knows whose.
left: Send them to the new office

text: The head of product proposes rewriting Meridian's product on Pulsar's stack in a month. Meridian's team finds out from your correspondence.
A Meridian employee says Pulsar people call him "the new guy," though he's been in the industry 15 years. It stings.
left: Have a word with the team

text: Finance presents a model in which the integration pays back in 18 years. The board was promised three. The model looks honest.
Security wants every Meridian employee on new laptops. Stock covers a third. The rest wait two months.
You're having lunch with two managers who don't speak to each other. They pass the salt through you. Food is going cold.
Pulsar's HR asks whether we could hold off telling Meridian about the bonus gap. "So as not to upset them." It's a sizeable gap.
Meridian's corporate cards got blocked in the switch to the new bank. Their sales team is on a business trip with no money.
On the metro you read staff feedback about you. One says: "Fair, but always looks exhausted." Hurtful or fair?
You finally make it to the barber. He asks what you do and tells you how his salon "merged" with the one next door. Want to hear it?
11 p.m. The overnight email migration is running and you're on call. The sysadmin writes: "Go to sleep if you like, we'll only wake you if there's a fire." Trust him?
The school parents' chat is discussing merging two classes. Someone writes: "We need someone who knows how this works." All eyes on you.
You realise you no longer sort people by former company. But your spreadsheet still has two columns. Delete one?
Your assistant writes late: "Tomorrow you have eight meetings, and one is with yourself. Who booked that?" You don't remember.
right: Delete it, add a real one

text: Walking your dog, you meet a neighbour who works at Meridian. He doesn't know who you are and talks about "the new integration person, who seems all right."
Your partner asks over dinner: "Can we have one evening without 'synergy' and 'duplication'?" Two minutes later you say "duplication."
Meridian's former CEO, now an adviser, calls at 8 a.m. proposing to "roll back a couple of decisions." He's still influential.
You come in at 7:30 to work in peace. A Meridian department head is already there and wants to "just talk while nobody's around."
right: Ask to do it at lunch

text: The new office map comes out. Meridian's department is labelled "Dept M," Pulsar's departments by full name. People are already asking why.
The risk manager sends an "integration risk heat map" this morning. It's entirely red. Even the "coffee machines" cell.
right: Forward it to the CEO as is

text: The regional office caretaker calls: "People with your new emblem want to take our sign down. Nobody told me." Let them in?
right: Ask them to wait till noon

text: The first joint project ships on time. The CEO praises only the Pulsar lead. He says nothing, though Meridian people did half the work.
right: Ask the lead to speak up

text: You receive 120 document templates, 60 from each company. Each is "definitely the best." Deadline for standardising: one month.
Staff vote on the new office colour: blue (Pulsar) or orange (Meridian). It's a tie. You have the casting vote.
L&D proposes a game: "Find a colleague from the other company with the same hobby." Winners get lunch. People snigger.
The external auditors ask about a line in the consolidated accounts: "Other — 3 million." Nobody remembers what it is.
The CEO wants a list of the "most valuable people" from both companies by Monday — "in case they start leaving." It's in your head, not on paper.
right: Write it alone at the weekend

text: Today you kept the key engineer. He's staying. You want to shout for joy, but you're on the metro. How to celebrate?
Tonight you're running a "How to talk about change" session for managers. You've talked about change all day. Your voice is going.
Your plumber neighbour explains how he joined two pipes of different diameters: "It's all about a good adapter." You nod thoughtfully.
Late evening, finance writes: "The retention bonus for key people was approved, but halved." People expect an answer tomorrow.
On the train you draft a thank-you letter to the integration team. It's two pages. Send it tonight or in the morning?
right: In the morning, after a reread

text: Accounting asks whose rules apply to receipts: Pulsar wants originals, Meridian accepts photos. Someone brought a printed photo of an original.
You look for the leave policy. Pulsar's wiki version is out of date; Meridian's sits on a page titled "Draft, do not read." Read it?
A folder appears on the shared drive: "FINAL_really_final_v3_Meridian_Pulsar_edits." Inside is the org chart only three people should see.
right: Find out who's seen it first

text: A new IT specialist hired for the integration asks on day one which systems matter. You show him a diagram with 34 arrows. He goes pale.
The CEO calls at 7:50: "I've changed my mind, we're keeping the name Pulsar." The new signs went up last night.
left: Ask him to sleep on it

text: The two chief accountants offer to share a desk "to agree faster." You suspect it might end in a calculator duel.
You fly to Meridian's regional office. At 8 a.m. they greet you with a welcome cake and a list of 40 questions. Your flight back is at 6.
The newsletter wants to interview you for a feature: "The Person Who United Us." Sounds grand. Agree?
left: Agree, but make it about the team

text: Pulsar and Meridian use different mobile carriers. Merging saves money but everyone gets new numbers. Sales is horrified.
A big client is ready to sign but asks who'll manage the account: the Pulsar manager or the Meridian one. Both are in the room.
You've been given an integration assistant. He's from Pulsar, and Meridian staff think he's a spy. So far he just brings you coffee.
The merged warehouse has identical parts under different codes. The same nut is listed as "N-14" and "Bolt_fix_M8." There are 2,000 of these.
left: Unify the catalogue in a month

text: Pulsar's quality team wants Meridian certified to Pulsar's standard. Two months of audits. Meridian already holds another, equally good one.
Meridian's chief accountant asks who signs off her sick leave now: you or Pulsar's CFO. She just needs an answer.
In a meeting the CEO suddenly proposes closing one of Meridian's business lines. You watch its head go pale.
Over lunch the lawyer says he's prepared 400 employment contract amendments. Each needs your signature. You have one pen.
HR wants "stay interviews" with all key people. There are 60, at 40 minutes each.
You notice that in the two marketing heads' feud, you prefer the one from Meridian. Will that bias your decision?
You're invited to a "Meet the Families" evening where staff from both companies bring their kids. It's your only free night.
Your brother calls to ask if he should join a company "about to merge with another." You laugh so hard he gets worried.
Making cottage-cheese pancakes in the evening, you think merging batter is easier than merging two support teams. They burn. Start over?
You're preparing a board presentation in the evening. Two months of integration in ten minutes. Every bullet is someone's drama.
You pick up the guitar you haven't touched since the integration began. Your fingers are rusty, but you feel lighter. Play on?
For three days you've been working out how to tell a good employee his role is going. He suspects nothing and jokes in the chat. How long can you wait?
An evening email from a Pulsar employee: "I used to fear Meridian, now we play volleyball together." You want to print and frame it.
Both HR teams independently sent a job offer to the same candidate this morning. With different salaries.
The budget committee wants integration costs cut 20%. You suggest cutting meetings. They suggest cutting training.
A supplier calls first thing: "We're getting orders from you twice. Send two lorries?" The volumes differ hugely.
You launch a daily one-emoji mood poll. Day one: Pulsar picks a smile, Meridian a straight face. Discuss it?
Meridian's secretary still gets tax office letters at the old address. She cycles them over to the new office.
You need to fly to Meridian's regional office for two days. Pulsar's annual report is due at the same time. Where are you needed more?
The merged sales team is being trained by two sets of trainers, each with their own method. Salespeople come out confused.
Meridian's counsel proposes keeping their legal entity another year "so the licences aren't disturbed." Finance hates double reporting.
The call-centre head wants a separate room for Meridian's agents: "They speak softly, ours are loud." There are no spare rooms.
Meridian's informal leader, whom everyone listens to, asks for a one-to-one. He wants to know "whether to encourage people to stay."
Designers argue over the new brand font: serif (Meridian) or sans-serif (Pulsar). Marketing wants "something in between."
For the first time in a month you open a novel. On page two the hero "unites two kingdoms." You shut it. Pick another?
Your allotment neighbour suggests combining plots for a shared vegetable garden. "You're the expert at this." You've never grown anything.
At 10:30 p.m. the CEO writes: "Can you meet Meridian's board at 8 tomorrow? No slides, keep it simple." You know "simple" never is.
It's the last day for three Meridian employees. They're meeting at a café tonight and invite you. You had a hand in their leaving.
Mum asks when you're finally coming to visit. "After the integration," you say. She asks when that is.
Marina from Meridian — the one with every process in her head — is back from vacation. At 9 there are six analysts with notebooks queuing at her desk.
left: Give her a week to write it down
right: Let her answer them all now

text: Igor from logistics sends a photo: the warehouse has two loading bays, Pulsar's and Meridian's. A lorry is parked between them; the driver doesn't know which to use.
Designer Anya asks for a week of quiet to finish the brand book. Seventeen people have already sent "small tweaks" this morning. Protect her?
Day one of the unified email. Half the messages arrived twice, three people lost their calendars, and the CEO can't find the Reply button.
Over morning coffee, HR confesses: "I don't know if I'm staying either." Her role duplicates Meridian's HR. She's the best you know.
Meridian's receptionist and Pulsar's now share one desk. Each greets "their own." Visitors are confused.
Finance shows the numbers: the coffee machines cost a small car a year. Proposal: one machine per floor.
You set up an "integration duty officer" anyone can bring questions to. Logically, the first shift should be yours.
Meridian's ex-CEO's card stopped working: his old role was abolished and the system "fired" him. He's standing at the turnstile.
In the new CRM, 2,000 Meridian clients have lost their managers' notes — birthdays, kids' names, "don't call on Mondays."
You're driving to a client with managers from both companies. In the car they argue over who speaks first. The client is 15 minutes away.
A Pulsar employee demands every process change go through committee, or "there'll be chaos." So far the chaos comes from the committee.
HR proposes an "exchange week": Pulsar staff work in Meridian teams and vice versa. Sales is appalled at losing a week.
Meridian's chief engineer shows their equipment is better. Moving Pulsar's production onto it means six months and double shifts.
Quarterly bonuses are calculated differently: Pulsar on revenue, Meridian on profit. This quarter one side gets more. Which?
You tour the warehouse with both companies' managers. Each explains why their racking is right. After an hour you've seen three racks.
A Meridian employee blogs about "life after the takeover." Funny and mostly kind. Legal is nervous.
left: Ask him to drop the name

text: You realise that through the whole integration you've never asked yourself what you want. It's 10 p.m. and the question hangs there.
Your downstairs neighbour turns out to be the merged company's new warehouse manager. He suggests "sorting a few things right here on the stairs."
A Meridian department head calls in the evening: "My people want to know if we keep our floor." The decision is a week away.
In the shower it hits you: merge the two procurement teams and make an analytics team from the freed-up people. Write it on the steamy mirror?
A friend calls from another city. You talk about work; he shows you his newborn. Suddenly your problems feel their true size.
Finishing the quarterly integration report. "Achievements": two pages. "Problems": six. Swap the order?
Painting a wall at home, you think: "At least one thing will be one colour." It comes out patchy. Repaint?
You realise you said "It's not my decision" five times today. They were your decisions. Own up tomorrow?
Pulsar's former COO, now "legacy adviser," sends a six-page email at 8 a.m.: "Mistakes You Are Making."
A courier brings a pile of contracts to sign. Half say Pulsar, half say the new name. Legal says both are correct.
right: Have them redone with the new name

text: Both companies' summer holiday rotas overlap so that in July the warehouse will be empty.
You visit a Meridian client to introduce yourself. He greets you: "I won't work with you until you bring Sergei back." Sergei quit on his own.
IT wants to move the servers Saturday morning. Someone has to sign the acceptance form. Your Saturday was free for the first time in a month.
At stand-up, Meridian's managers say "we" meaning their old company; Pulsar's mean the new merged one. You notice the difference.
right: Don't make a thing of it

text: Both companies ordered year-end client gifts. Some clients will get two: one from Pulsar, one from Meridian. Different logos.
At the cooler you hear that "the new sales head from Meridian got the job because he's friends with the CEO." You know that's false.
HR asks you to fill in a competency grid for every manager. Forty-eight competencies, including "Ability to hold a pause."
The new shared warehouse opens. The first stocktake shows Pulsar counts boxes, Meridian counts units. Stock levels are 12 times reality.
A Pulsar employee refers a friend for a role. Meridian used to pay referral bonuses; Pulsar didn't. He asks about the bonus.
The CEO wants to shut Meridian's "pet project" — eco packaging. It loses money, but the team lives for it.
You're offered a company-paid "Change Management" course. Saturdays, eight weeks. You are change management right now.
Today, for the first time, you raised your voice in a meeting. Two managers fell silent, and the problem got solved. But you feel uneasy.
Your kid draws "You at Work": you're holding two offices on strings like balloons. Stick it on the fridge?
You're drafting the "Integration Week in Review" bulletin. You want to write "All going to plan," but the plan changed three times. What do you write?
At a family dinner your mother-in-law describes how two collective farms merged in her youth. "The key was a shared bathhouse." You consider one for the office.
At 9 p.m. the CEO sends the new org chart for sign-off. A department you promised to keep is missing.
You notice you're smiling walking past a department that used to be all Pulsar. Now a mixed team is arguing about pizza. Is that success?
You're watching an office sitcom. A character says: "We're merging, everyone's losing it." Funny and a bit sad. Binge the season?
Your phone bill arrives: 40 hours of calls this month, 35 about the integration, half after 7 p.m.
A Pulsar employee writes: "Sorry it's late. Could I not be moved into the joint department? It scares me." She's excellent.
You signed up for swimming to switch off. The coach says: "You need to integrate your arms and legs." You laugh into the water. Keep going?
In your drafts: an email to the CEO, "We need more time." You've been writing it for three weeks. Send it today?
The counsellor suggested keeping a "good things" list. Today's entry: "Both accounting teams had cake together." Add more?
Staff from both companies are playing evening volleyball, one player short. They call you over. You're in a suit, after 11 meetings.
For the first time you introduced yourself to a stranger without mentioning work. It came out as "I… like walks." A good start?
HR sends the numbers: nine people left this month, seven from Meridian. The board will ask tomorrow.
An old friend asks why you haven't called in ages. You start on the two companies and stop yourself: she asked about you.
At a team dinner, someone from Meridian raises a toast to Pulsar. Silence. Then Pulsar toasts Meridian. Your turn?
At 10 p.m. your laptop insists on installing the new corporate system update. Two hours. Tomorrow at 9 you present from this laptop.
You dream of endlessly changing the building's signs, and they keep changing back. You wake up determined. What happens this morning?
At a late-night shop you meet Meridian's accountant. She's buying a cake: "for tomorrow — one year working with your lot." Join in?
Pulsar's assistant asks to move to a Meridian team: "They respect assistants more." Pulsar's whole paperwork rests on her.
First thing, the CEO says you're "too soft" and it's time to "show who's boss." You think things are actually working.
A Meridian newcomer fills in Pulsar's HR form. "Previous company" is mandatory, and the only option is "Pulsar."
Pulsar's IT director wants to speed things up by cutting off Meridian's email from Monday. Nobody told the people on vacation.
At the morning coffee break three Meridian people ask when the new business cards are coming. It's the most peaceful question all week.
Today you announce Meridian's department is moving to Pulsar's floor. Meridian asks why not the other way round. Fair point.
Client survey results: 60% didn't even know about the merger. Good or bad?
In the lift the CEO asks you, in 20 seconds, to "settle the two warehouses for good by lunch." It's been going three weeks.
A Pulsar client calls at 8:15: "I got an invoice with the new logo but the old bank details. Where do I pay?" Accounting's still asleep.
right: Ask him to call back at 10

text: On the commute a leadership podcast says: "A leader in change is the one who stays calm." You're late and anxious.
The warehouse got new uniforms. The logo on the back is upside down. Three hundred sets. The crew says they like it.
At a meeting two teams each present the department's future. They contradict each other on every slide. Both are excellent.
Veterans from both companies have formed an "elders' council" and want to advise the integration. They're already writing minutes.
It's fridge-clearing day. Two-month-old yoghurts labelled "Meridian, hands off" are found. Their owner has left.
The leasing manager says Pulsar's old office can be sublet, but it must be empty in two weeks. Forty people are still there.
The new brand's ad needs staff from both companies. Thirty from Pulsar signed up, nobody from Meridian.
Ordering pizza for a two-team meeting. Pulsar wants pepperoni, Meridian vegetarian. Order for thirty.
The merged IT team asks for one boss. Pulsar's candidate is a strong engineer; Meridian's is a strong manager.
At an all-hands the CEO jokes: "Well, Meridian, welcome to a real company." Only Pulsar laughs.
right: Have a word with the CEO

text: The new office is short of chairs: Pulsar got office chairs, Meridian got stools. The second delivery is a month away.
Pulsar starts meetings on the dot; Meridian starts five minutes late "so everyone's there." Your first joint meeting: at 10:00 the room is half empty.
A Pulsar employee admits he "fought" a Meridian manager over one client for ten years. Now they're supposed to sit together. He asks to be moved.
The sales director pitches an "internal contest" between ex-Pulsar and ex-Meridian teams. "Healthy competition!" You doubt the word "healthy."
An accident makes you late. Everyone waiting for your first meeting — where you announce the new managers — is already there and nervous.
The office manager proposes a cross-company Secret Santa: everyone gives a gift to someone from the other side. Budget: a small sum.
The merged team's new lead is from Meridian. At 9 he comes to you: "I don't think they listen to me." He's right; you've seen it.
The canteen till only accepts Pulsar passes. Meridian staff pay cash in a separate queue. A long one.
The culture working group proposes a ritual: every Monday everyone says one nice thing about the other company. It sounds like a punishment.
Two secretaries take minutes at integration meetings. Their versions differ on the key point: who owns what. The CEO reads both.
An HR audit finds three people at Meridian in the same role on different pay. Five at Pulsar. What now?
Your Meridian deputy asks you to teach him to present to the board. "Meridian never had a board." Coaching takes your lunches all week.
The CEO asks you to "quietly" draft a scenario for closing one of the offices. Not even your team can know.
Managers from both sides are dividing clients. One is left that nobody wants: pays late, calls often. Each wants the other to have him.
Meridian's buyers order "just in case"; Pulsar's order "exactly to plan." The warehouse is overstocked for six months.
Legal is merging two ethics codes. Meridian bans gifts worth more than a chocolate bar; Pulsar more than a book. Where's the line?
The CEO wants "one team" by New Year and proposes a three-day off-site for all managers. Half of them object.
HR emails that two of your "key people" have offers from competitors. Both told you themselves. What do you do?
At 11 p.m. you're scrolling job ads. Not for yourself — checking what competitors pay your people. Time to stop?
You've signed up for evening dance classes. Your partner works at Meridian and keeps stepping on your toes, apologising "on behalf of the whole company."
Your partner proposes a rule: no phones at dinner. Five minutes in, your pocket buzzes. Could be the CEO. Could be spam.
You're signing year-end cards for staff. 400 of them. By number 200 your hand is aching, and you want something personal in each.
You count: in three months of integration you've had two full days off. Both sick days. The conclusion is obvious.
left: Take a day off this week

text: Evening quiz night with mixed teams. Yours is called "Synergy and Pies." You know the merger question, but it's not your turn.
You reread your first integration deck. You promised "full integration in three months." Three months have passed.
The retired neighbour on the bench asks why you always come home so late. "In my day we were home by six." He's right.
Morning pilot of the shared ticket system. First ticket: "Someone bring back the old system." Signed: "Everyone."
An employee returns from vacation to a different office: his department moved, his desk is taken, the company has a new name. He's in the lobby with a suitcase.
right: Send him to the office manager

text: Someone mistakenly emailed the pay tables for both companies. Meridian paid more. The office is buzzing.
Accounting starts closing the first joint month. Pulsar's chief accountant says: "I can't close by their rules." Meridian's says the same.
left: Pair them up for a week

text: You host a breakfast for both management teams. A Meridian manager has brought homemade pies. Pulsar clearly wasn't expecting it.
Meridian's courier asks where to get paid now: he always collected cash at the till. Pulsar has no till.
left: Help him open a bank card

text: Pulsar works from the office five days; Meridian two. Pulsar's managers demand Meridian come in full-time.
The consultants propose a "quick win": merge the call centres over a weekend. You've seen the call centres. Not a quick win.
A journalist calls to check if the merged company has "new lunch break rules." Trivial, but it sounds like a scandal.
You receive "Values of the Merged Company" for approval. The word "synergy" appears 14 times. You counted.
At CRM training it turns out the trainer used to work at Meridian and praises their old system in every example. Pulsar is rolling its eyes.
Meridian staff show how they close deals in a week rather than a month. Pulsar listens, sceptical but curious.
Today you caught yourself defending Meridian to Pulsar as fiercely as you once defended Pulsar. Are you one of both now, or of neither?
right: Talk it over with a mentor

text: In the evening chat your team is swapping integration memes. One is about you. It's funny and kind. React?
You cook dinner from two recipes — grandma's and one from the internet. Odd, but tasty. A sign?
At 9:30 p.m. the analyst sends a report: "The merged company's sales beat the two old ones combined for the first time." You want to wake the CEO.
You're in pyjamas when the sysadmin calls: "There's a Meridian server nobody knew about. It's been crunching reports since 2015." Go in?
right: Ask him to switch it off till morning

text: At a school reunion everyone shares their successes. You describe merging two procurement teams. A classmate asks: "And that counts as success?"
A meeting is cancelled and suddenly your evening is free. First thought: finish the warehouse plan. Second: you haven't been to the cinema in ages.
An employee whose role was cut writes: "Thanks for telling me honestly and early. I've found a new job." You feel both relief and sadness.
right: Ask for feedback on the process

text: You realise you haven't praised your Meridian deputy all week, though he carried two tough meetings. Message him now?
Two managers are arguing about the stationery budget in the group chat. Everyone's watching. It's 10 p.m.
The family wants an evening bike ride. Your handlebars still sport a Pulsar sticker from last year's company day. Peel it off?
In the evening you look at the redundancy list. Next to one name: "back from maternity leave a month ago." Reconsider?
The CEO asks this morning: "Can we announce the integration is complete?" You know there are six months to go. He wants good news for the board.
New ID badges are handed out. Half of Meridian's surnames are misspelt: Pulsar's system didn't handle certain letters.
The new turnstile only admits one face every ten seconds. At 9 the queue reaches the street. Security suggests opening the gates.
Your plan for the day: 9:00 "Coffee machine final," 11:00 "CRM final," 2:00 "Brand final." Each "final" has been postponed twice already.
Procurement wants a single water supplier. Pulsar likes sparkling; Meridian still. One supplier for everything.
You find someone's CV on the printer this morning. From the font, someone at Meridian. Thirty copies.
The morning after the first joint party. A photo in the chat shows both CEOs dancing. Pulsar's CEO asks for it to be deleted.
right: Ask to keep it — it's sweet

text: Pulsar uses one courier firm, Meridian another. Customers get orders in two boxes from two couriers.
A Meridian employee brought a "peace pie" to the Pulsar team her group has argued with all week. The pie is gone; the argument continues.
left: Seize the moment for a meeting

text: Marketing launches the "Stronger Together" campaign. The first video is shot in an office where the teams still sit on separate floors.
left: Seat everyone together for the shoot

text: The process audit shows Meridian approves a contract in 2 days; Pulsar in 14. Pulsar says theirs is "more robust."
The shared printer breaks on quarter-close day. Pulsar has a spare, but it's "for our people." Meridian's accounting is desperate.
Security proposes colour-coded passes: blue for Pulsar, orange for Meridian. "For convenience."
The CEO wants you to run a workshop for everyone: "How We Merged." You're not sure you have yet.
A client complains that he hears "Welcome to Pulsar" and then gets transferred to Meridian with different hold music.
The canteen now has a "friendship table" for mixed lunches. On day one only the office manager who came up with it sits there.
You haven't seen a sunrise in a month because you get up after it, or a sunset because you're in a windowless room. Change something?
A big Meridian client calls at 8 p.m.: "I hear my new manager doesn't know my business. Should I move to a competitor?"
The family plays a city-building board game. You propose merging two cities into one. Everyone objects. Give in?
At 9 p.m. the CEO writes: "The board praised you today." You can't remember the last time anyone did. Reply?
On your evening run you pass a Pulsar and a Meridian employee jogging together and arguing about the CRM. Overtake or join?
In the evening you clear out the Meridian cabinet that's now yours. Inside: a box of thank-you letters from clients over 20 years.
left: Keep them for a company museum

text: Your builder neighbour says knocking two flats together is the hardest renovation: "You can't knock down the load-bearing walls." You think of the two accounting teams.
You launch a morning poll: "What's getting in your way since the merger?" Top answer: "Polls." Cut back?
In the morning meeting Pulsar's CEO and Meridian's ex-CEO both say "I propose" at the same moment. Everyone looks at you to moderate.
You drop in on a Meridian team stand-up. They fall silent and start reporting to you like the boss. They used to joke around.
left: Ask them to carry on as usual

text: On the shuttle you sit next to Meridian's driver, who now drives everyone. He tells you which Pulsar people never say hello.
Your kid asks you to take him to school this morning. It's 40 minutes, and you'll miss the start of the warehouse meeting. He rarely asks.
Meridian never clocked in; Pulsar uses fingerprint scanners. Meridian staff refuse to give fingerprints.
One warehouse's lease expires in a month. Renewing is pricey; moving takes ages. The warehouses aren't merged yet.
Your assistant politely notes you've answered 600 emails this week. "Shall we delegate?" he suggests.
The seating council proposes seating people "by project, not by company." That means 120 people moving in a single day.
It turns out all Meridian staff still get Pulsar's customer discount newsletter. And use the discounts.
You're handed a ring of 60 keys to Meridian's offices. None labelled. The new office manager expects you to sort it out.
Both coffee machines break the same morning. For the first time the office is united: everyone queues together at the café downstairs. Fix them right away?
left: Fix them tomorrow — let them mingle

text: Today the company's name changes officially. The CEO wants to cut a ribbon this morning. There's no ribbon, only tape.
Employees' credentials for client visits must be reissued. Meridian has 80, Pulsar 140. New ones will take a month.
A Meridian employee comes to you in tears: her team was dissolved and she doesn't know who she reports to. You're late for a meeting.
Meridian's former CEO invites you to breakfast "to get to know each other, no ties." You know he wants to talk about his people.
First day running one warehouse instead of two. By lunch, Pulsar and Meridian loaders have found common ground: they're both complaining about the new system.
Legal discovers Meridian owes a supplier a penalty for early termination. Big penalty. The contract was terminated for the integration.
The joint marketing head role opens. Both former directors apply. One is stronger; the other is loved by the team.
Staff vote on which coffee machine stays. Meridian's wins by two votes. Pulsar demands a recount.
A major customer invites you to present the new brand at their offices. The brand book isn't ready, but they want it "by Thursday."
