HR brings a "rumour report." The most popular: Meridian's office will be sold to become a shopping mall. False, but plausible.
New hires since the merger go through two induction courses, Pulsar's and Meridian's. They contradict each other.
The CEO takes you to lunch and asks who you'd fire if you had to fire one person. He wants a name.
The warehouse reveals Meridian stored Pulsar's products for three years and billed for it. Pulsar paid.
Today you had an unhurried lunch for the first time in a month, and nobody died. In fact the afternoon meeting went better.
You're about to send the new structure email to all staff at 11 p.m. If it goes now, people will read it at night.
You settle down with a book. Your deputy calls: "Not asleep? Five minutes?" Five minutes usually becomes an hour.
right: Ask him to wait till morning

text: On your run you meet the CEO. He's faster and pitches "a few integration ideas" mid-stride. You have no breath to answer.
At midnight you realise the two support teams could be merged by request type, not company. Brilliant idea. Wake your deputy?
At parents' evening the teacher describes merging two classes. The kids became friends in a week, through football. Note it down?
You realise the integration's best ideas came not from you but from people in the warehouse and support. Tell them?
Your old Pulsar boss, who left five years ago, calls: "Heard you're integrating. Advice: don't rush the people part." Timely advice.
Your Meridian deputy sends a photo: him with Pulsar colleagues at the bowling alley. Caption: "Look, we're friends."
right: Ask for it for the newsletter

text: You set your alarm for 5:30 to prep for the board before work. Your partner looks disapproving. Prepare now instead?
The "Jupiter-Samara" meeting room (the compromise name) is under repair. Your client meeting is in an hour. Only the kitchen is free.
IT announces it has merged all group chats into one. Now it has 900 members and 4,000 messages before lunch.
You open the integration task list: 412 items. Thirty more were added this morning. Strike out the stale ones?
Investors want to tour the office and "see the integration." Half the office is still in boxes. They arrive at 10.
All of Pulsar's blue mugs have vanished. Suspicion falls on Meridian. This morning they turn up: they were taken to a dishwasher that only runs on Fridays.
Two employees come to you with a conflict: one Pulsar, one Meridian. Half an hour in, it turns out it's about the window seat, not the companies.
right: Use it as a case study

text: Finance is reconciling receivables. One client owes Pulsar, and Meridian owes him. The amounts nearly match. Now it's one company.
At a pricing meeting it emerges Meridian sells the same product 15% cheaper. Pulsar's clients will soon find out.
The CEO asks you to teach him the new messenger. He wants to "send voice notes like everyone else." The lesson will eat your lunch break.
Veterans propose a "history corner" in the lobby for both companies. It needs display cases, and the budget's been cut.
left: Do it on a wall for free

text: The unified website goes live today. "About us" still contains the draft line "Pulsar is the leader — Meridian isn't."
You feel more tired than ever before. But tomorrow is the final CRM decision. Book a day off after?
At a friends' dinner the host's company is also merging. You trade experiences all evening. The other guests are bored.
The neighbour's cat has come round again. You joke that you've "integrated" her. The neighbours don't laugh and ask for her back.
At 10 p.m. the lawyer writes: "All signed. Legally you're one company now." You've waited six months for this. How do you celebrate?
You can't sleep, remembering the faces of the people you had to let go. All found jobs, you checked. It's still heavy.
Pulsar's mascot is a robot; Meridian's is an owl. Marketing proposes a "robo-owl" for the new brand. The sketch is terrifying.
The new website needs a founding year. Pulsar dates from 1998, Meridian from 1994. Each side wants theirs. Marketing needs an answer by 10.
Meridian has 40,000 social followers; Pulsar has 4,000. Pulsar's marketing wants a "fresh start." Meridian objects.
The facilities manager reports 6,000 pens with Pulsar's old logo and 4,000 with Meridian's. Binning them feels wasteful; handing them out feels odd.
Morning fire drill. Pulsar heads to the north exit, Meridian to the south, following their old plans. The security chief despairs.
Clients ask what happens to their points: Pulsar has bonuses, Meridian has discount cards. The call centre has been saying "we'll check" all morning.
You and a Meridian accountant share the same extension: 214. You've had two calls about invoices already this morning.
Both companies supported different causes for years: Pulsar animal shelters, Meridian children's libraries. The budget covers one programme.
The companies have nearly identical products under different names. Pulsar's salespeople pitch against Meridian's product.
Pulsar reviews staff once a year, Meridian quarterly. Meridian's promotions are already scheduled for this month.
Two corporate libraries have been merged. Every leadership book is there twice. Books on mergers: none at all.
Pool cars: Pulsar has white saloons, Meridian orange hatchbacks with its logo. Repainting is pricey; driving around with Meridian's logo is odd.
An employee who's worked at both companies has become an unofficial "translator," explaining Meridian's habits to Pulsar. He loves it, but his own work is stalling.
Legal asks you to read 15 key Meridian contracts by Friday. Each is 40 pages of small print.
A Meridian veteran retires a week after the merger. He wants his send-off "our way, with an accordion." Pulsar doesn't do that.
You organise a tree-planting day for both companies. Sixty volunteers signed up. There are twenty shovels.
A great Pulsar employee was due for promotion this month. His new role now duplicates one at Meridian. He's waiting for news.
In the evening you count how many people thanked you today. Three. How many did you thank? Two. Even it up?
The nursery calls: you need to pick up your child an hour early. That's when you're meeting two directors about merging departments.
Friday. The merged team suggests going out together for the first time — without any push from you. Join, or let them enjoy it boss-free?
You step out into the rain. The Meridian-branded umbrella you were given this morning breaks after three steps. A sign?
left: Laugh and walk in the rain
right: Go back and wait it out

text: Writing the evening progress report, you're tempted to add charts to make it "weighty." You have 14. Are they needed?
Choosing a holiday gift for your Meridian deputy. Something unifying — a book about Pulsar? A blanket with the new logo? Or just nice tea?
The budget meeting has run until 9 p.m. You can tell nobody will decide anything in the next hour. Stop?
Making a playlist for the drive home. First song: "two lonely people who found each other." Your brain immediately thinks of the two accounting teams.
Meridian's ex-CEO calls late: "I hear you kept my mentoring programme. Thank you." He's clearly moved.
Today someone from Pulsar said "our Meridian." You're not sure you heard right. Is this what it was all for?
The shared leave system goes live today. A third of staff see their leave balance reset to zero. Panic in the chat.
A sign in the lobby counts "Days without inter-company conflict." This morning it says 0. Yesterday it said 3.
Comms wants you to record a video message for staff. You hate cameras, and the script opens with "Dear colleagues, we are a family."
left: Record it in your own words

text: At 8:30 it turns out Meridian's salaries went to old accounts the bank has already closed. The money comes back in 5 days.
A young Meridian employee proposes automating the two companies' report consolidation. He built a prototype over the weekend. It works.
right: Hand it to IT to finish

text: Monday. The week begins with an email: "Still no decision on coffee machines; we need your vote." You thought this was closed.
right: Send it back to a vote

text: Finance shows the merger's costs to date. A fifth went to consultants who wrote "merge the companies."
Eating a sandwich on the walk between offices, you're caught by a Pulsar employee asking if his department is being moved to Meridian.
A consultant draws an "integration map" across a whole meeting-room wall. A week later it's out of date. Redraw it?
You publish new joint travel rules. Within an hour, 80 questions. Half begin "But we used to…"
Meridian's strongest team lead says he'll stay if his team isn't broken up. The plan says it gets broken up.
Pulsar's KPI is call volume; Meridian's is customer satisfaction. In the merged team some call a lot, others talk long.
You realise you're as tired of the integration as anyone. Only you can't show it. Or can you?
An evening with no calls. Your phone's been silent for two hours. You've checked three times whether it's broken. It isn't. Enjoy it?
The board assigns you an "integration mentor." He suggests meeting daily at 7:30. You already sleep five hours.
HR wants 200 transfer orders signed by 10 a.m. You notice half have the departments mixed up.
HR suggests starting the day with joint exercises in the courtyard. Day one: you and three people from Meridian.
The CEO sees two sales plans this morning. Combined, they exceed the entire market. He asks you to explain.
A courier delivers flowers for "the integration lead" from Meridian's team. The note: "For not breaking our warehouse." You're touched.
Disaster this morning: someone from Pulsar posted "Good morning" in the all-staff chat. Three hundred people replied.
The regional office calls at 8: "Our warehouse keys stopped working — the locks were swapped to Pulsar's." A truck is waiting.
First thing, your Meridian deputy admits he's thinking of leaving because he "never became one of us." You need him.
right: Give him a project to lead

text: The naming meeting enters its third hour. Someone suggests "Pulseridian." Done that. Someone else: "MeriPul." Also done.
The merged support team has closed its first week with no complaints about "ping-pong" between teams. The head asks to celebrate.
You're bidding as the merged company. The client requires "at least five years' experience." The merged company is a month old.
A sign in the lift says "Meridian marketing has moved to floor 7." It moved to floor 5. People keep going to 7.
The customer service head wants to keep two call centres: "Clients are used to the voices." Expensive, but possibly true.
The anonymous suggestion box got 48 notes this week: 30 about parking, 10 about coffee, 8 about you.
In the new shared canteen Pulsar and Meridian staff sit at separate tables. You arrive with your tray. Where do you sit?
right: At an empty one, invite all

text: IT shows the two systems are held together with "temporary hacks" that could collapse any moment. Rewriting takes three months.
For the first time in six months you sent your last email at 6 p.m. and shut the laptop. Home feels oddly quiet. Turn it back on?
At a party two managers argue loudly about which company was better. You're standing right there.
Friends invite you out, and for the first time in a month you don't talk about work. Though you were tempted twice. A victory?
The CEO calls in the evening: "The board wants to speed up. Can we finish in two months instead of six?"
Your musician neighbour is playing piano. You recognise the tune — Meridian's office party song. Ask how he knows it?
Writing up the day: coffee machines — keep both; CRM — chosen; name — postponed. Not bad?
The family suggests a holiday in the city where Meridian's regional office is. "You can pop in while we're there." Suspiciously convenient.
Someone called you "our integrator" today, warmly. It feels like recognition. And you know the work isn't done.
A client writes: "Your new manager is better than the old one." The new one is from Pulsar, the old from Meridian. Forward to both?
left: Forward to the new one only

text: Eating a sandwich at 11 p.m. in front of your laptop. On screen: "Employee wellbeing: action plan." The irony isn't lost on you.
The board asks you this morning to present "the integration's biggest mistake." You know it: rushing the warehouse merger. It was your call.
You learn your best Pulsar person is moving to the joint strategy team. It's a promotion. But you need him.
The new logo goes up on the building today. Staff from both companies stand outside together, taking photos. Together, for once.
The CEO can't send an email to the board: the new mail system flags the word "merger" as spam. The board is waiting.
Morning managers' check-in. Two from Meridian are missing: they're "at a farewell breakfast for the old office."
The recruiter asks which company name to post jobs under. Candidates know Meridian better, but it's going away soon.
The call centre needs one script for client calls. Pulsar's is 20 seconds; Meridian's is 2 minutes, including weather chat.
You need a date for the company day. Pulsar celebrated in May, Meridian in September. Someone proposes keeping both.
The quarterly report has one revenue line instead of two for the first time. Finance from both companies gathers to admire it like a newborn.
Meridian's warehouse shift hands over to Pulsar's using a logbook. Pulsar doesn't have one; they hand over verbally.
It's Meridian's 30th anniversary. Formally the company no longer exists. Staff want to celebrate. The CEO thinks it's "weird."
You realise you wanted both Pulsar and Meridian to like you. Didn't happen. But you were honest. Is that better?
You get home at 9:30 p.m. Dinner's cold; the family's eaten. A note: "Heat it up. We're proud of you." You could cry.
A Pulsar employee emails: "Why did Meridian colleagues get new laptops and we didn't?" They were issued on the security schedule.
The office PA plays its first announcement: "The company welcomes you." The voice is the robot from Pulsar's demos. Meridian winces.
Friday morning, two managers argue over who chairs the weekly meeting. Both have sent invites for the same time.
The analyst shows turnover has fallen since the departments merged. A first since the integration began. Announce it?
A Meridian employee asks to pin a photo of his old team by his desk. "To remember." The office manager is against "personal photos."
The unified business cards have finally arrived. All of them show Pulsar's old office address, which everyone has left.
A new Pulsar team lead heading an ex-Meridian team asks: "They do everything their own way, and their results beat mine." Your advice?
The tax office calls asking why the company has two postal addresses. Meridian's accountant is explaining but mixing up dates.
Team-building budget: Pulsar wants go-karting, Meridian a baking class. Not enough for both.
At the printer two staffers argue whose turn it is. Each insists they hit Print first. The printer spits out a third job: someone's 2019 report.
On a video call with regional offices, half the participants — Meridian's — can't connect to the new conferencing system.
HR wants a test on the new company values. Wrong answers mean "retraining." Staff are already joking about exams.
Pulsar's team eats soup together every Thursday. Meridian's team asks to join. Pulsar hesitates.
The merged sales team finishes its first month 10% above the old teams combined. The CEO proposes raising the target 30%.
A Meridian employee can't book leave: her service was reset in the new system. Officially she's "new," though she's been here 12 years.
In a meeting today you heard a Pulsar person defend a Meridian person's idea for the first time. Mark the day?
An employee writes at 10 p.m.: "Sorry, can't sleep. Is it true the old departments are being dissolved for good?" Reply now?
The CEO takes you to dinner and spends half the evening reminiscing about his early Pulsar days. He clearly misses the old company.
You're doing a 1,000-piece jigsaw with your kid. Two pieces from different sets fit perfectly. Your kid is thrilled.
At 8 p.m. finance urgently needs sign-off on a payment to a Meridian supplier. You were planning to end that contract.
On an evening walk you meet two employees — one Pulsar, one Meridian — walking their dogs and talking about… dogs. Not work.
Revisiting the duplicate roles list in the evening. Half are settled. The hardest remain: where both people are excellent.
Reading the staff comments book in the evening. One entry: "Too many emails from the integration lead." That's you.
Mum calls: "You sound different. Has something changed?" She's right — a lot has. Tell her?
Former Meridian staff who left after the merger are meeting up tonight and invite you. You're responsible for some of their departures.
Your cat lay on the keyboard again and sent "ffffffff" to the group chat. Forty people reacted. Delete it?
The joint task board launches today. Pulsar calls items "tickets," Meridian calls them "assignments." One word is needed.
A journalist asks how many people lost their jobs after the merger. The number is small, but any number will make a headline.
Every computer updated to a new operating system overnight. Meridian doesn't know it. Forty people are hunting for the Start button.
HR advises "a box of tissues in every meeting room" before the structure announcement. You hope that's a joke.
First morning in the new shared office. You arrive at 8 to find everyone already there — sitting mixed together. On their own.
You accidentally bring your old Pulsar pass. The new Meridian guard doesn't know you and won't let you in. On principle.
The CEO announces he's leaving in a month. The board asks you to stay on as the key person during the transition.
Approving the holiday calendar. Meridian's region has a local day off; Pulsar's doesn't. Everyone wants it.
Legal reports the formal merger has slipped a quarter over one registrar's signature. All documents must be redone with the new date.
A client wants one team, not two. Your Pulsar and Meridian managers still run his account on separate plans.
right: Put them together for a week

text: Facilities proposes saving on stationery: "Let people bring their own pens." At Meridian they already did.
You ask both teams for feedback. Pulsar says "too soft." Meridian says "too harsh." What now?
For the first time you don't know what to do at the weekend, because there's no weekend work. The integration runs itself. Worrying or wonderful?
The first joint engagement survey is in. Meridian scores 20 points lower. Comments say: "Nobody listens to us."
right: Publish the figures and a plan

text: The new racks were built to Pulsar's spec, and Meridian's forklifts don't fit between them. By two centimetres.
Trial seating by project today. By 10, three Pulsar people have drifted back to their old desks "out of habit." Those are now taken.
right: Give them a week to adjust

text: At the morning review it emerges a big order fell between the two CRMs. The client's been waiting since Monday. Both sides are hunting for someone to blame.
The designer brings 90 pages of brand guidelines. "How not to use the logo" takes up 40. Approve?
An elderly Meridian client is at reception, here "as always, to hand over papers in person." He can't understand where his company went.
Pulsar and Meridian launched near-identical promotions at the same time. Clients got both.
The CEO tries Meridian's coffee in the kitchen and says out loud: "Excellent! Why didn't we have this?" Pulsar freezes.
left: Pick it up with a joke

text: You get a cost-saving idea: merge the two HR teams and cut three people. One of them is the person who came up with it.
Meridian's salespeople learn Pulsar pays bonuses from the first sale, Meridian from the fifth. They want "the Pulsar way."
A dispute over shared-drive folders: by client (Pulsar) or by year (Meridian). It's been raging in the comments for three days.
You propose joint training for both companies' managers. Pulsar signs up eagerly; Meridian asks: "Is it mandatory?"
A former rival of both companies proposes a partnership: "You're big now — let's be friends." The CEO is thrilled; legal is horrified.
Security finds a sticky note with three system passwords on a Meridian desk. The employee says: "We always did this, we're all friends."
Meridian's drivers want to keep their old orange uniforms: "Clients recognise us in them." The new uniform is grey.
You reread your very first integration note: "People come first." Lately you've thought more about systems. Back to basics?
In the evening you stumble on a three-hour documentary about two carmakers merging. Watch it?
You're invited to an evening talk: "Integration: what we've learned." The speaker is a consultant who never attended one of your meetings.
The team sends a voice note: they've sung "We Are One Now" to the tune of Meridian's old song. It's awful and touching.
A finance friend asks how you calculate synergies. You explain; he laughs. "Where I work, we call that hope."
Cooking dinner, you combine leftovers from two pots. It becomes something new. The family loves it. You see a sign.
A retiring Pulsar veteran writes in the evening: "Thank you for letting me see two houses become one." Reply?
right: Invite him to a farewell lunch

text: Friday. You write yourself three questions for next week. The first: "Who at Meridian still feels like an outsider?"
Your deputy calls at 9 p.m.: "I've decided to stay. Thanks for the project." You exhale with relief. Keep it short?
You think: in six months no one will remember which company they came from. They'll remember how they were treated. Were you kind enough?
The new head of the merged warehouse wants both old procedures scrapped: "We'll write our own from scratch." That's a month's work.
The only lift is broken this morning. Pulsar sits on floor 9, Meridian on 2. The meeting is on 9.
You discover you're on 63 mailing lists across both companies. Two hundred emails every morning. Unsubscribe from half?
A Meridian supplier comes to meet you with a cake bearing Meridian's old logo. Meridian staff are moved.
The CEO is late for the all-hands. The hall is full; both companies are waiting. You're asked to "keep them busy."
New CRM training is set for 8 a.m. so it won't disrupt work. Pulsar staff normally start at 10 and see it as "punishment."
The Pulsar and Meridian reporting teams submit their first joint report with zero errors. The CEO didn't notice — there were no errors to notice.
The first new hire who knows neither Pulsar nor Meridian arrives. People ask "Whose are you?" He doesn't understand the question.
The merged IT helpdesk opens one hotline. First caller: the CEO. The printer isn't working. It isn't plugged in.
A big Pulsar client is celebrating an anniversary. Pulsar used to give gift hampers, Meridian books. What does the new company give?
Accounting files Meridian's final standalone report. The chief accountant asks for five minutes to "say goodbye" to it. Everyone waits.
All day today nobody mentioned Pulsar or Meridian. Only the new name. You notice only in the evening.
You can't remember the last time you read anything but procedures. On the shelf: a novel you got for your birthday a year ago.
Over dinner your partner asks what happens when the integration's over. You realise you've never thought about it. Think now?
A Meridian employee writes: "Can I tell the all-hands how we merged the archives? It was hilarious." Give her the floor?
The board schedules an 8 p.m. call: "Integration — first six months." You've prepared for a week. Nervous?
Your kid's cartoon shows two anthills uniting against the rain. "Like at your work?" he asks. You nod.
The group chat is silent tonight. Not a question, not a complaint. You suspect something's broken. Check?
Your fitness band says: "Your stress level is down 20% on last month." You're not sure it's true, but it's nice.
You spot a social media poll: "Which was better, Pulsar or Meridian?" One of your staff started it.
Today you said "I don't know" in a meeting for the first time, and nobody fainted. Someone even said "Thanks for being honest."
The Meridian client who threatened to leave writes: "I'm staying. Your new manager knows my business better than the old one."
In the courtyard kids are playing "merger": two teams join forces against a third. It seems your daughter taught them.
Your last email of the day: "Thanks, everyone, for this week." You want to add a line about each person. That's another hour.
The cashier at a late-night shop asks why you're out so late. "Integration," you say. She nods: "They merged two of our stores too."
Sunday, 8 p.m. You're preparing Monday's presentation. The family calls you for a movie. The deck is almost done.
The CEO sends an evening voice note: "I want to say thank you. We couldn't have done it without you." Eight seconds. A brevity record.
Overnight the link between the two inventory systems broke. This morning shipments have stopped. Drivers are waiting at the gates. Where are you needed?
HR reports three Meridian staff refuse to sign new contracts. They object to the remote-work clause.
The merged team has come up with its own department name. It's funny, and they love it. Approve?
Your calendar has two meetings on the same topic: one set by Pulsar, one by Meridian. Same attendees.
You fly into the regional office. Meridian's founder's portrait still hangs there, next to last year's calendar. Staff watch for your reaction.
Your assistant asks which emails she can answer on your behalf. You've always answered everything yourself. Delegate?
The merged team's stand-up took ten minutes for the first time. Nobody said "we used to." Praise them?
Shareholders want to see the "real savings" from the merger. So far the main one is lower rent. The rest is planned.
Pulsar's courier and Meridian's courier arrive at the same client with documents at the same moment. The client calls you, laughing.
Today's verdict on coffee machines: keep both, on different floors, each shared by everyone. Announce it with humour?
Meridian comes in four days a week instead of two for the first time. The car park is overflowing and the coffee machines can't keep up.
Six-month integration review. Each manager must name one success. The warehouse head says: "We stopped swearing at each other."
The CEO suggests "refreshing" the new logo in six months. It was just installed on every building.
A competitor openly poaches your salespeople, promising "the stability you don't have." Two have already gone for interviews.
The culture consultants deliver their report: "The merged company's culture is a hybrid." Three months' fees for that word.
After the integration you're offered the COO role. It's a promotion, but you'd hoped for a breather.
right: Ask for three months off first

text: A "thank-you wall" has appeared in the kitchen. Forty notes in a week, from staff of both companies thanking each other.
You're giving the board a tour of the merged warehouse. Midway, a Meridian forklift rams a Pulsar rack.
At a working meeting two managers agreed on something without you for the first time. They present the decision. It's good.
The new passes have stopped working in the canteen. Everyone eats on the company until it's fixed. Accounting is in shock.
A Pulsar employee comes up and admits: "I was against the merger. Now I think I was wrong." He asks you to keep it quiet.
You catch yourself saying "us" and meaning the whole merged company. No quotation marks. When did that happen?
right: Don't make a thing of it

text: The two companies' cleaners can't agree on floors. One cleans "the Pulsar way" — fast; the other "the Meridian way" — thorough.
The Pulsar veteran who vowed to "outlast you" brings you a coffee this morning. "I've been thinking — you're all right," he says, and walks off.
An industry magazine calls your merger "one of the calmest of the year." The CEO sends it to everyone. You know how many storms there were.
A client asks why his invoice has two logos. Accounting forgot to update the template. It's gone to fifty more clients.
Monday. Meridian's team has amended the "Silence = productivity" poster to read "…and biscuits." Pulsar doesn't object.
Finance wants the merged report format approved. Twelve tabs proposed. The CEO only reads the first.
A new hire is late on day one: he went to Pulsar's old office, as stated in the welcome email. You wrote that email.
On the shuttle, staff from both companies are singing along to the radio. The driver asks you to "do something." You're in the back row.
right: Ask them to keep it down

text: The risk director says the "culture clash risk" can be downgraded from red to amber. A first.
Pulsar's trophy cabinet stands in the lobby. Meridian's awards are in a box in storage — and there are more of them. Meridian staff ask where they are.
Morning presentation to both teams. The projector won't see your laptop. IT says "Meridian projectors are different."
The follow-up engagement survey: Meridian now trails by 5 points, not 20. A comment: "It's got better."
The merged company's new bank wants to "meet the leadership" at 8 a.m. tomorrow. You have a board meeting at 8:30.
The department door finally has its new sign: just the new name, no Pulsar, no Meridian. Someone has drawn a heart underneath.
The CEO calls: "The board wants you to speak about the integration at an industry conference." It's in a week.
You propose scrapping all Friday-afternoon meetings — "time to actually work." Both companies vote yes unanimously. A first.
At lunch, managers from both companies discuss their vacations, not the integration, for the first time. You're itching to raise the budget.
The warehouses are officially merged. The warehouse head suggests a tour for all office staff "so they see where the hands-on work happens."
You must write to an employee whose role isn't in the new structure. HR's template sounds cold. Rewrite it?
left: Rewrite it in your own words

text: The merged sales team asks to bring back the old team names: "Pulsar South" and "Meridian North." They say it's easier to navigate.
You learn an important integration meeting happened yesterday without you. Good decisions were made. You feel a bit left out.
right: Ask to be invited next time

text: Pulsar's salespeople are teaching Meridian's cold calling; Meridian's teach them account care. No plan at all.
The air-con breaks mid-meeting. Meridian sighs in relief: finally warm. Pulsar takes off its jackets.
The first external audit of the merged company. The auditor says: "Remarkably clean for a merger like this." You can't believe your ears.
The CEO floats a new task: "Since you merged two companies so well, shall we add a third?" He's joking. Probably.
A Meridian employee offers a workshop on her planning method. Thirty sign up, twenty of them from Pulsar.
One duplicate role remains: two office managers, both wonderful. One volunteers to leave: "I've wanted to study for ages."
The magazine wants a wrap-up interview: "How it really went." You want to be honest, mistakes included. PR objects.
You notice you're joking in meetings again. The last time was before the integration. A good sign?
The team holds a "How We Merged" evening, showing funny chat screenshots from the early months. Half are about you.
Your brother calls: "So, is your merger over?" You think about it. Formally, no. In your gut — almost.
At 10 p.m. a Meridian employee sends a voice note: "Sorry, I just wanted to say I enjoy working here again."
For the first time in six months you cook something elaborate. It takes two hours. Your phone is in the other room.
You're writing your conference talk: "How to Merge Two Companies and Keep Your Sanity." It's honest and funny in places.
Before heading home you find a gift from the merged team on your desk: a mug that reads "Chief of Coffee Machines."
Your neighbour shows you a local paper article about your merger. "Is that you? I thought you were an accountant." Explain?
Today your team settled three disputes without you. Don't they need you anymore? Or is this what success looks like?
The final integration committee meeting. Members propose not disbanding it, but "renaming it the development committee."
On your evening run you aren't thinking about work for the first time. Just your breathing, and that spring is coming. One more lap?
At dinner your kid asks: "When will you start coming home on time again?" You say: "From Monday." Will you keep your word?
You're writing the all-staff email: the integration is officially complete. You want to thank each person by name. There are 400.
Drinking tea late at night, you remember day one of the integration. It seemed impossible then. Write down what you learned?
The anonymous channel posts a "leak" tonight: Pulsar staff will supposedly move to Meridian's lower pay. It's invented, but the panic is real.
At 7 p.m. accounting says some Meridian staff will be paid a day late due to the new system. People have gone home.
Your swim coach says: "You swim like you're towing someone." He's right — you're towing two companies. Relax your shoulders?
At midnight the sysadmin writes: "The shared server's down. Back by morning, but the warehouse can't ship until 10." Wake the warehouse head?
Old Pulsar colleagues invite you out tonight, "like before, just us." No Meridian. You're pleased and uneasy at once.
right: Go with the old crowd only

text: You must decide by morning who heads the merged accounting team. Both candidates are strong. Both messaged you tonight "just to see how you are."
You realise you haven't seen your parents in two weeks, though they live twenty minutes away. Can the integration wait one evening?
Pulsar's chief accountant writes late: "Sorry I grumbled. The new system really is better." Her first such admission in six months.
In the evening you doubt choosing Meridian's CRM. Pulsar is still grumbling. Revisit the decision?
You join an evening art class. First assignment: "draw two objects that became one." You draw two coffee machines.
The board asks tonight for next year's budget to be recalculated "for the new structure" by morning. That's an all-nighter.
On a walk a friend says: "You don't say 'them' anymore, you say 'we.'" You hadn't noticed. Happy or thoughtful?
You finally book a holiday. A minute later an email arrives: "Those are the dates of the merged company's audit." Cancel?
Meridian's coffee supplier offers to supply beans for both machines, discounted. Pulsar's supplier hears and bids higher.
In the lift queue a Pulsar employee lets a Meridian employee go first. She thanks him. A minute later they're arguing about the CRM. Step in?
Meridian's former CEO calls: "My old clients are complaining about the new delivery times." He no longer runs anything, but they still call him.
left: Ask him to route them to you

text: The morning email wishes happy birthday to a Meridian employee who left a month ago. She replies: "Thanks, unexpected."
The analyst shows Meridian's clients have started buying Pulsar's products. The first real synergy. The CEO doesn't know yet.
The new head of a merged department — from Meridian — asks if he can change half of Pulsar's processes. He's sure it's better.
right: Ask him to start with one

text: HR organises a morning "One Team" run. Fifty people take part. At the finish it turns out the T-shirts carry Pulsar's old logo.
A Pulsar employee asks why Meridian had a gym and the new office doesn't. It was in the basement of Meridian's old building.
Pulsar's guard complains Meridian staff don't show their passes — they just wave. "That's how they did it."
This morning you notice an item on your list unrelated to the integration: "Book a dentist appointment." It's been there since spring.
Accounting closed the month in three days instead of seven, for the first time. Both chief accountants are having coffee together, looking pleased.
Designers argue the new blue is too close to Pulsar's. Meridian asks for some orange. The brand book is due tomorrow.
The merged company's talent pool: 12 from Pulsar, 11 from Meridian. Nearly even for the first time. Announce it?
The consultants invoice for "cultural integration support." One line: "coffee machine brainstorming" — 40 hours.
New parking rules: spaces by lottery, not seniority. Pulsar's veterans are outraged; Meridian's youngsters delighted.
Interns from both companies teamed up and built a project everyone loved. They ask to stay together after the internship.
A client posts a public review: "Service improved after the merger, but invoices arrive twice."
Two departments are still preparing the same report for the CEO. Each thinks it's the only one.
Dress code vote: Pulsar wants casual, Meridian wants business. It's 50/50. Yours is the deciding vote.
A Pulsar partner and a Meridian partner end up in the same meeting and discover they were competing for the same contract. Now they're on the same side.
You cancel every "sync on the sync" meeting. Six hours a week freed up. The CEO asks what you're doing now.
A key Pulsar person is leaving despite the bonus. "It's not the money, I'm just tired of change." You understand.
Quarter results: revenue up, turnover down, but more complaints about coffee machines. What goes in the headline?
The CEO decides to take the new CRM training himself — publicly, on the big screen — and gets lost in the buttons. Help?
Today nobody cried, quit or quarrelled. You check your email to see if you missed something. No. Just a good day.
You ask the merged team what bothers them most. The most honest answer: "We still don't know who signs off our leave."
right: Put it on the monthly plan

text: Meridian's regional office asks for no calls before 11 — the time difference. Pulsar loves 9 a.m. calls.
The CEO emails everyone: "We are one company." A minute later half of Meridian's auto-replies come back: "I'm on holiday."
right: Ask him to send it again

text: Legal brings news: you've bought the trademark from the bakery. In return the bakery wants boxes supplied at cost.
In the lift a Meridian employee says out of the blue: "You know, I used to be scared of you. Now I think you're just very tired." Reply?
The warehouse morning report: zero shipping errors all week, a first. The warehouse head asks for "a team bonus, even a token one."
At a client's this morning, two sales teams show two different decks on the new product. The client asks which one is right.
Tuesday, 8:30. Someone has put a "Peace Ambassador" sign on your desk. You suspect accounting.
A courier brings a box from Meridian's regional office — papers that "should have been sent at the merger." They're original contracts.
left: Go through them with legal now

text: A Pulsar client complains the new Meridian manager is "too polite and too slow." The client likes speed.
left: Brief the manager on his style

text: Morning phishing drill: "URGENT: new structure, click here." Forty percent of both companies clicked.
The CEO says he wants to "spend more time with people." He asks you to draw up a weekly schedule of department visits.
Two managers want your analysts for the same week. Both projects matter; the managers come from different former companies.
Quality proposes scrapping half of Pulsar's inspections, since Meridian has no more defects without them. The quality veterans are offended.
You take a mixed team on a client visit. On the way it emerges everyone has a different idea of the visit's purpose.
Two teams argue over the better client email template. You propose a test: which one gets opened more.
Facilities wants to refit the shared kitchen. It'll be closed a week. Coffee machines too.
You launch an ideas contest: "How can we work better together?" Idea one: "Cancel idea contests." Idea two is good.
A Meridian employee asks to move to an ex-Pulsar team where his friend works. That team's head is fine with it. You'd lose a person.
right: Ask him to wait a quarter

text: A consultant proposes a "process satisfaction audit." You already know the result: nobody likes any process.
In a client meeting your Meridian manager says "we at Meridian." The client corrects him: "You're one company now, aren't you?"
The IT systems meeting runs till 8 p.m. Final question: what to call the merged database. Suggestion: "Database."
Your deputy calls in the evening: "I'll tell the team about the cuts myself. They should hear it from me." Trust him?
The evening news covers another firm's failed merger: "The staff never found common ground." You switch off the TV.
The Pulsar intern you once reassured writes: "I got hired permanently! Thanks for being honest back then."
At night you remember you never decided where Meridian's piano goes. It's been in the corridor a month.
right: Leave it, everyone's used to it

text: Dinner at your parents'. Dad asks if everyone became friends after the merger. You laugh: "Almost."
HR sends a draft onboarding programme. It includes "Introduce newcomers to Pulsar's history." Meridian's is missing.
Friday evening. For the first time in six months you didn't take the laptop home. You feel strangely light.
Your sister calls: her company has announced a merger. "You know how to survive this, right?" You do.
Today you couldn't remember which coffee machine belonged to whom. Integration success, or exhaustion?
On an evening call the board asks: "What next?" You prepared numbers, but you want to talk about people.
You're on the last train home. Two staffers, one Pulsar, one Meridian, who stayed late, are asleep on each other's shoulders.
In the evening you read a profile of yourself in the company magazine: "The person who got two companies talking." You want to show your mum.
You book a two-week holiday. Your deputy writes: "Go, we'll manage." You believe him. Almost.
Late in the evening you pass Meridian's old office. The lights are on: the new tenant is a children's art school. Take a look?
The day's tally: two disputes settled, one person retained, one coffee machine broken. By integration standards, a great day.
Stuck in traffic, you get a call from the warehouse head: "Both shifts turned up at once, old schedule and new. Who works?" You're an hour away.
right: Ask them to wait for you

text: The printer delivers 20,000 new letterhead sheets. The tax number is wrong. You need them for contracts from today.
HR asks whether to drop "Former company" from the new staff directory. Many want it gone; some object.
Nobody was late to the joint stand-up for the first time. You suspect the new biscuits Meridian's team has started bringing.
The road to the new office is closed. Meridian staff on the shuttle are stuck. Pulsar walked from the metro.
The board wants the report to include "integration lessons for future deals." You think the main one is "don't rush the coffee machines."
You walk in to find the new CFO in your office. He's been put there "temporarily." Your desk is now by the window.
HR reports a Meridian employee wants his old title back: "The new one sounds like a demotion." Same pay.
Ten people from both companies are queuing at the coffee machine, chatting away. You're late for a meeting, but you need coffee too.
This morning you must decide which of two warehouses to close. One is closer to clients; the other is cheaper. Both crews await the news.
On your desk: a card from Pulsar's team — "Thanks for not letting us dissolve." Next to it, from Meridian — "Thanks for not letting us be swallowed."
On your morning rounds you notice Meridian's old logo clock still hangs on their floor. It's five minutes slow.
HR's latest "rumour report." This week's top rumour: you're leaving. You're not. Deny it?
The two teams' first joint release ships with a bug. Pulsar says it's Meridian's code; Meridian says the opposite.
Managers argue whether bonuses should count "contribution to the integration." Nobody knows how to measure it.
Staff want to name the new office kitchen after the cleaner who's worked at both companies for 30 years. She's embarrassed.
At lunch you find the canteen has two menus today: "Pulsar" and "Meridian." The cook decided to "please everyone."
The CEO wants one company goal for the year. Each side has sent ten. You need one.
An employee you thought hated the integration is leaving — not because of it: he's opening his own bakery and invites everyone to the launch.
The seating council proposes a weekly "sit anywhere day." The office manager is horrified.
Investors ask for the integration's most surprising result. The honest answer: "People started having lunch together." It sounds flimsy.
The CEO wants a slide: "The Integration Year in Review." You want just one photo: a mixed team at the coffee machine.
You're asked to onboard a new team acquired from a third company. The CEO says: "You've got experience." You laugh. He doesn't.
The Meridian veteran who threatened to retire over the new system is teaching youngsters how to use it today. He's pleased.
The board asks you to assess the CEO's performance during the integration. He doesn't know.
The new CRM is down for two hours. Staff from both companies are cursing it together in the chat. You notice: together.
For the first time you're thinking not about how to merge, but what to do with the merged whole. That's a different job. Are you ready?
Your family proposes a new tradition: Sunday board-game nights, no phones. That's when you usually plan your week.
The Meridian client where it all began calls late: "Just wanted to say — you pulled it off. I'm staying another three years." You smile.
Your old Pulsar boss writes: "Heard the integration worked. I'm proud." You want to send a long reply.
You realise the integration taught you to say "no" to the CEO, "yes" to rest and "thank you" to people. Not bad at all.
A Meridian colleague sends an evening photo of the new joint team on an outing: "Remember how scared we were of each other?"
right: Ask to use it in the newsletter

text: At home you finally decide to finish the renovation you started before the integration. Your partner laughs: "Go on, merge the two rooms."
The CEO writes in the evening: "Let's discuss your next role tomorrow." You're not sure you're ready for more mergers.
Before bed you reread your diary from the integration's first days. Back then you wrote: "I can't do this." You want to add a note in the margin.
Your Meridian neighbour, out walking his dog, says: "Now I know who you are. Thanks for keeping it fair." The dogs sniff each other.
The team throws an evening party to mark the end of the integration. You're asked to speak. You prepared for a week, but want to go without notes.
Evening. You sit in the kitchen drinking tea from your "Chief of Coffee Machines" mug. The phone is silent. The integration is over; the work isn't.
A friend calls to invite you hiking at the weekend. For the first time in a year you don't check your calendar before saying yes.
You write a letter to yourself a year ahead: "If there's another merger — start with the people, and keep both coffee machines." Schedule it?
At 9:05 two managers argue whose greeting goes on the phone line: Pulsar recorded a peppy one, Meridian a calm one. Clients hear both in turn.
Meridian's storekeeper with his notebook and Pulsar's young logistician with a tablet count the same pallet. The numbers match. Both are amazed.
An electronic queue for accounting goes live. Meridian is used to popping in "for a minute." The minute lasts half an hour.
You find someone moved Pulsar's desks closer to the windows overnight. Suspects: the cleaners and marketing.
The CEO decides to sit in the open-plan area "for unity." Everyone around him has stopped talking. Ask him to go back to his office?
Legal brings the merged company's charter to sign. Clause 1.1 has a typo in the company name. Registration is at 11 today.
The kitchen is closed for cleaning. No coffee in any machine. The office looks like a zombie film. Run out for coffee for everyone?
A client writes: "Finally one contract instead of two! But why did you send it three times?" A mailing system glitch.
New visitor rules start today: guests wait 20 minutes for a pass. An important partner is in the lobby, already texting the CEO.
At stand-up, a Pulsar manager proposes scrapping Friday reports. A Meridian manager unexpectedly agrees. Everyone looks at you.
The glass display cases for the companies' "history corner" were smashed at the warehouse. The new forklift route is to blame.
HR says eight of ten interns want to stay with the merged company. There are five places.
Over coffee the CEO asks what you'd do differently if you started the integration again. He's taking notes.
Ex-Pulsar and ex-Meridian departments independently booked two venues for the year-end party. Deposits paid on both.
IT wants to name the main server after the cat who lived in Meridian's server room. The cat moved with the server.
In the evening you realise you miss the old Pulsar, quirks and all. And Meridian, which you barely knew. Is that normal?
Meridian's team invites you to their last "Friday tea" in the old format. From Monday it's for everyone. You're tired.
Finance reports the integration cost 12% more than planned. The CEO hasn't seen it. Call him now?
The kids want a bedtime story. You start one about two dragons sharing a cave. By the end the dragons are drawing up a cleaning rota.
The guard who knows your favourite tea texts: "You left at 6 today. I'm proud." You laugh out loud.
A message arrives at night from the regional office — it's morning there — asking if the joint party will include them too.
